content.content:
1	Citation in APA format: Schweitzer, M. E., Krueger, K. L., Boothby, E., & Cooney, G. (2025).
2	Negotiation. In D. T. Gilbert, S. T. Fiske, E. J. Finkel, & W. B. Mendes (Eds.), The handbook of social
3	psychology (6th ed.). Situational Press. https://doi.org/10.70400/NUZE7621
4	Negotiation
5	Maurice E. Schweitzer, University of Pennsylvania
6	Kori L. Krueger, Morgan State University
7	Erica Boothby, University of Pennsylvania
8	Gus Cooney, University of Pennsylvania
9	Many of our most consequential outcomes derive from negotiations—from the price we pay for
10	homes and cars, to the salaries we earn, to quotidian outcomes such as which household chores we
11	perform, where we go on vacation, and what vegetables our children eat. Though the negotiation
12	process and the nature of negotiated outcomes vary profoundly across contexts, several
13	fundamental features apply to every negotiation.
14	Negotiation is a communication process between two or more parties with conflicting and
15	convergent interests, including at least one party who is seeking to reach an agreement (Carnevale
16	& Pruitt, 1992; Fisher et al., 2011; Kang et al., 2020; Neale & Bazerman, 1992; see Boothby et al., 2023;
17	Bazerman, et al., 2000; Thompson et al., 2010 for reviews). This chapter provides an overview of
18	negotiation scholarship and focuses on both the stable features of negotiations across contexts and
19	the primary sources of variability.
20	Every negotiation is characterized by distinctive phases. This review includes the key phases of a
21	negotiation: Setting the stage, communicating, closing, and post-negotiation behavior. Each section
22	highlights key inputs and outcomes of the aforementioned phases and discusses how these phases
23	build upon one another. It is important to note that although humans have negotiated for millennia,
24	empirical academic investigations of negotiation began in the 1960s. Extant negotiation scholarship
25	is reviewed, and promising areas for future study are identified—such as opportunities to study
26	negotiations in the field and with artificial intelligence.
27	In this review, negotiations are conceptualized as a social interaction. Despite regularities and
28	common features of negotiations, social interactions represent a highly complex and unpredictable
29	human activity. As a result, negotiations reflect this complexity; specifically, both the negotiation
30	process and negotiated outcomes are shaped by different personalities, cultures, idiosyncrasies of
31	verbal and nonverbal expressions, the influence of emotion and trust, the unfolding dynamics of
32	conversation, and the influence of situational factors. This review highlights historic and current
33	psychology and management scholarship that addresses key features of this social interaction.
34	Much of this work documents how variability in features such as emotion can alter the negotiation
35	process and negotiated outcomes. Reviewing this work offers a broad understanding of negotiation
36	scholarship and highlights opportunities for future scholarship to increase our theoretical
37	understanding of negotiations and the prospect of negotiating more successfully.
38	PHASES OF NEGOTIATION
39	This review identifies four phases of negotiation (see Figure 1): Setting the stage, communicating,
40	closing, and post-negotiation behavior. In this review, each phase is considered in turn. Importantly,
41	many negotiations occur over extended periods of time and involve repeated rounds of negotiation.
42	As such, though these phases represent a useful framework for conceptualizing the negotiation
43	process, in practice, negotiations rarely follow a perfectly linear path as they progress from one
44	stage to the next. In addition, the extent to which negotiators spend time in each of these phases
45	may vary considerably across contexts—and across negotiators.
46	The first phase of negotiation involves setting the stage. In general, negotiators who prepare (e.g.,
47	gathering information ahead of time, identifying key questions, and considering others’
48	perspectives) outperform those who do not (Fisher & Ury, 1981; Thompson & Leonardelli, 2004;
49	Thompson et al., 2010; see also Helmold et al., 2022; Malhotra & Bazerman, 2007; Thompson, 2015).
50	However, both the amount and the type of preparation may vary considerably across negotiation
51	contexts and individuals. For example, a crisis negotiator may be unable to prepare before they start
52	negotiating; instead, they may seek to gather information during the communicating phase.
53	This review introduces an important negotiation classification in relation to preparation: Disputes
54	versus Opportunities. Dispute Negotiations, negotiations triggered by a conflict in which one or
55	more parties suffered a loss, are distinct from Opportunity Negotiations, negotiations triggered by
56	the opportunity for one or more parties to improve their status quo. Disputes occur within the
57	shadow of power (e.g., going to court), are triggered by a specific event (e.g., a divorce), and are more
58	likely to be characterized by linked outcomes, a shared history, and high emotion. Some Disputes
59	afford parties substantial preparation time (e.g., divorce negotiations), but the time between a loss
60	and the start of a Dispute Negotiation may be relatively short. For example, when a server spills
61	coffee on a patron or when a hotel fails to find a customer’s reservation, individuals may begin a
62	negotiation before they spend much time preparing. Opportunity Negotiations, in contrast,
63	typically allow negotiators to plan for the negotiation (e.g., preparing for a conversation to discuss a
64	potential new partnership).
65	The second negotiation phase is communicating. This phase has received the most scholarly and
66	popular press attention. Here, negotiators perform three important tasks: They engage in non-task
67	communication, exchange information, and exchange offers. By engaging in non-task
68	communication (e.g., “Welcome to my store” or “How was your trip?”), negotiators can build rapport.
69	By exchanging information (e.g., “How long has this property been on the market?”), negotiators can
70	identify opportunities for an agreement and shift leverage. Subsequently, by exchanging offers (e.g.,
71	“How about $3.2 million?”), negotiators can search for a potential agreement.
72	In the third phase of negotiation, the closing phase, negotiators commit to an agreement (or
73	recognize that they have failed to do so). This may involve a ritual (e.g., a handshake) or a formal
74	document (e.g., a signed contract). In this phase, negotiators make decisions about the specificity and
75	flexibility of their agreement, and they either signal their commitment to the deal or reach an
76	impasse.
77	Finally, there is the post-negotiation phase. After reaching an agreement, negotiators may continue
78	to interact with one another (e.g., after hiring a new recruit or contracting someone to perform a
79	service). This phase typically involves the creation of measurable value, and the negotiation process
80	can shape this important, but largely overlooked (by scholars), negotiation stage.
81	Figure 1: Phases of Negotiation
82	Note: The negotiation process is characterized by several different phases. Often (but not
83	always), negotiators prepare for a negotiation prior to initiating the negotiation process. The
84	decision to initiate a negotiation is a critical step in setting the stage for mutual consent.
85	Communication typically begins with non-task communication (e.g., informal chitchat),
86	proceeds to the exchange of information, and concludes with an exchange of offers. However,
87	these three phases of communication may occur in any order. Negotiations culminate in the
88	acknowledgement of an agreement (e.g., a handshake or a signed contract), followed by post-
89	negotiation behavior (e.g., satisfying the deal or planning a follow-up negotiation).
90	Though each negotiation phase can profoundly shape outcomes, negotiation research has largely
91	focused on the exchange of offers and the exchange of information phases. As a result, we know
92	surprisingly little about setting the stage, closing, or post-negotiation phases of the negotiation
93	process.
94	To build their understanding of negotiations, scholars have relied heavily on a roleplay negotiation
95	paradigm. In this paradigm, experimenters recruit participants online, to a behavioral laboratory, or
96	in a classroom setting; subsequently, they provide participants with background information to
97	play a role (e.g., a one-page write-up that prepares them to be the seller of a painting); participants
98	are then paired with a peer or confederate (e.g., someone who will play the role of a buyer of a
99	painting) and complete the communicating phase of negotiation (typically via text or face-to-face);
100	finally, they submit an agreement sheet that allows scholars to assess the economic value of the
101	agreement (see Jang et al., 2018; Boothby et al., 2023).
102	This experimental paradigm is well-suited to investigate certain questions about the
103	communicating phase of negotiation (e.g., how people respond to different types of questions in a
104	negotiation), but ill-suited to many other questions that remain underexplored, such as how the
105	negotiation process influences post-negotiation behavior, how long-term relationships influence
106	negotiations, and how perceived high stakes influence negotiations. As a result of the heavy
107	reliance on a single paradigm within the negotiation literature, there are substantial gaps in
108	scholars’ understanding of negotiations.
109	The ensuing sections of this chapter describe the key features of the four negotiation phases. Each
110	section concludes with the key questions that remain unanswered within that phase.
111	Phase 1: Setting The Stage
112	Relatively few studies have investigated this phase of negotiation. The work that has investigated
113	setting the stage identifies several activities that people should undertake before starting a
114	negotiation. This includes identifying the type of negotiation they are in, deciding to initiate or
115	accept a negotiation, knowing when not to negotiate, gathering information, developing a BATNA
116	(best alternative to a negotiated agreement) and aspiration price, setting goals, perspective-taking
117	about the opposing party, considering who is negotiating, identifying the key issues of the
118	negotiation, considering one’s mindset, and planning ahead (e.g., preparing a response to what they
119	might be asked, planning to make concessions).
120	Recognize And Identify Negotiation Type: Dispute Vs. Opportunity
121	One key preparation step negotiators should take is to recognize the type of negotiation they are
122	facing (see Table 1 for a typology of negotiations). Much of the existing negotiation scholarship has
123	focused on Opportunity Negotiations. In these negotiations, parties approach each other without a
124	history of conflict or loss, and they seek opportunities to improve their status quo.
125	In contrast, a vibrant literature in legal scholarship under the broader umbrella of Alternative
126	Dispute Resolution (ADR) has studied negotiations that reflect Dispute Negotiations. In Disputes,
127	one or more parties, having suffered a loss, may approach a counterpart seeking redress. These
128	negotiations, compared to Opportunities, are more likely to be characterized by conflict and intense
129	emotion.
130	In Opportunity Negotiations, parties explore opportunities to create value. For example, in an
131	Opportunity Negotiation, a seller could gain cash from selling their used couch, whereas a buyer
132	could gain access to inexpensive furniture, or two companies may expect to benefit from a merger.
133	In these cases, negotiators have the opportunity to end up better off than they were before the
134	negotiation took place.
135	In contrast to Opportunity Negotiations, Dispute Negotiations follow from a disagreement or a
136	failure (Thompson, 2015; Ury et al., 1988; Ury, 1993). For example, following poor service, a customer
137	could seek redress by negotiating a discount. Or, if a neighbor’s dog bites a young child, the child’s
138	parents could ask the neighbor to repair the situation (e.g., by paying for a doctor’s visit). Dispute
139	Negotiations can resolve (or exacerbate) the dispute. Legal scholars conceptualize Dispute
140	Negotiations as occurring “within the shadow” of going to court; that is, if the negotiation process
141	fails, the disputants may go to court, and each party’s anticipated costs and benefits of going to trial
142	create the space for an agreement (Coursey & Stanley, 1988; Gross, 2018). When negotiators in a
143	Dispute Negotiation focus on their underlying interests, rather than focusing on their power, they
144	are more likely to conceptualize the negotiation as an Opportunity Negotiation.
145	Though little negotiation scholarship has highlighted the distinction between Opportunities and
146	Disputes, this distinction is important for several reasons. First, Disputes and Opportunities
147	generally elicit different emotions during a negotiation. For example, whereas disputant negotiators
148	may start a negotiation feeling angry, opportunity negotiators are unlikely to experience
149	frustration before they begin a negotiation (though they may express anger during a negotiation,
150	for strategic reasons; see Section on Expressing Anger). Second, opportunity and dispute negotiators
151	may differ with respect to their BATNAs and the possible actions that are available to them outside
152	of a negotiation. Opportunity negotiators have the option to seek agreement with other interested
153	parties if the present negotiation fails. In contrast, disputants may focus on an interaction with a
154	particular counterpart (e.g., the neighbor with a dog), and opportunities to negotiate with other
155	parties may be less relevant. Further, disputants are far more likely to consider taking legal action if
156	they cannot come to an agreeable outcome. Finally, negotiators in these two classes are also likely to
157	differ in their goals. Opportunity negotiators generally strive for the best deal for themselves (or for
158	both parties), with a focus on maximizing gains, whereas dispute negotiators are more likely
159	focused on seeking redress and making amends. In some cases, disputants (e.g., divorcing spouses)
160	may even prefer outcomes that are costly to the other side, even if they derive little or no benefit
161	from the concessions themselves.
162	Table 1: Types of Negotiations
163	Note: Rather than dichotomies, many of these distinctions represent continuums.
164	Decision To Initiate, Accept, And Persist In A Negotiation
165	A critical but understudied antecedent to negotiations is the decision to initiate a negotiation. In
166	some cases, the opportunity to negotiate is relatively obvious. For example, some sellers invite
167	buyers to give them their “best offer.” In other cases, the opportunity to negotiate is less obvious, as
168	the dominant paradigm scholars have used to study negotiations overlooks the actual decision to
169	negotiate. For instance, scholars often give participants background materials and instruct them to
170	negotiate; consequently, we know very little about when or how people recognize the opportunity
171	to negotiate (or initiate a negotiation) (see Small et al., 2007 for an exception).
172	Another underexplored area of research is the decision to accept an invitation to negotiate. When
173	deciding whether to accept such an invitation, each party needs to assess their counterpart’s
174	intentions. Sincere negotiators enter a negotiation seeking to reach an agreement (Kang et al., 2020).
175	In contrast, Insincere negotiators enter a negotiation seeking to use the negotiation process to
176	achieve an ulterior motive (see Table 1). For example, an insincere negotiator may hope to learn
177	proprietary information, stall for time, or create a positive impression (e.g., show that they are
178	willing to cooperate when they have no intention of actually reaching a negotiated agreement).
179	Surprisingly, most negotiation scholars have assumed that people enter negotiations with the intent
180	to reach an agreement. In fact, many canonical definitions of negotiation explicitly state this
181	assumption (Fisher et al., 2011; Mislin et al., 2011; Rubin & Brown, 2013). Other work, however—and
182	many lawsuits—reveal that insincere negotiations are pervasive and that the decision to enter a
183	negotiation is an important strategic decision in itself (Kang et al., 2020).
184	Only a handful of studies have addressed the important questions of when negotiators should
185	initiate a negotiation (Bear et al., 2024), when they should avoid a negotiation (Kang et al., 2020;
186	Hart & Schweitzer, 2020), and when they should exit or persist in an existing negotiation (Kang et
187	al., 2020). In some cases, people should negotiate more; in other situations, they should negotiate
188	less.
189	The extent to which someone should negotiate more or less will be informed by expectations and
190	opportunities. First, prospective negotiators need to understand the negotiation norms and
191	expectations of their unique situation. These factors will vary across cultures, contexts, and
192	counterparts. For example, most employers expect prospective employees to negotiate—but some do
193	not (Labitoria, 2022). Second, prospective negotiators need to consider the costs and benefits of
194	negotiating. When the context is complex, the opportunity to learn about negotiators’ underlying
195	preferences is great, and the stakes are high, people are generally more willing to negotiate because
196	they are more likely to identify opportunities for joint gains. In other cases, entering a negotiation
197	may be costly. For example, when a counterpart does not expect to negotiate and the negotiation
198	involves the delivery of a service (Hart & Schweitzer, 2020), initiating a negotiation may harm the
199	relationship and ultimately harm a counterpart’s post-agreement motivation when they deliver the
200	service. For example, aggressively negotiating with a new babysitter may harm their post-
201	negotiation motivation to do a great job when they are babysitting.
202	In practice, many people negotiate less than they should. The most common emotion people
203	associate with negotiations is anxiety (Brooks & Schweitzer, 2011). Though anxiety can motivate
204	people to prepare for a negotiation, it can also prompt them to avoid or exit a negotiation
205	prematurely (Brooks & Schweitzer, 2011). There are several concerns that may trigger anxiety in
206	these situations: When people enter a negotiation, they may place their current agreement at risk
207	(Galinsky & Schweitzer, 2015), they may harm their relationship with their counterpart (Hart &
208	Schweitzer, 2020), or they may make a costly concession (Maaravi & Levy, 2017). In many cases,
209	however, these concerns are overblown (see Hart et al., 2024). For example, after employers extend
210	offers to prospective employees, some candidates may fear that if they attempt to negotiate, the
211	employer will withdraw the offer. However, research comparing the employer’s perspective with
212	that of the prospective employee indicates that job candidates have inflated concerns about the risk
213	of losing an offer by initiating a negotiation (Hart et al., 2024).
214	Negotiator concerns about harming relational outcomes and making costly concessions are
215	legitimate (Hart & Schweitzer, 2020), but certain strategies can help to mitigate them. Specifically,
216	when it comes to impacting relational outcomes, how people negotiate matters more than whether
217	they negotiate. For example, by learning about norms, communicating in person, developing
218	rapport, and asking questions, people who choose to negotiate may be able to enhance, rather than
219	harm, their relational outcomes.
220	In conclusion, future scholars should investigate the decision to initiate a negotiation, accept an
221	invitation to negotiate, and persist in a negotiation. These are important yet substantially under-
222	studied questions.
223	Gathering Information
224	Prior to initiating a negotiation, each party should gather information about the context, their
225	alternatives, and their counterpart. Gathering information prior to a negotiation is usually critical
226	(Fisher & Ury, 1981; Thompson & Leonardelli, 2004; Thompson et al., 2010; see also Helmold et al.,
227	2022; Malhotra & Bazerman, 2007; Thompson, 2015). Though there is limited scholarship on this
228	topic, research suggests that a lack of preparation is a common negotiator mistake (see Fisher et al.,
229	2011; Malhotra & Bazerman, 2007; Thompson, 2015).
230	Even with extensive preparation, however, there are times when negotiators can only learn
231	important information from their counterpart during the negotiation process. For example,
232	negotiators may need to ask their counterpart what they are willing to pay or what their future
233	intentions are. In these cases, negotiations are characterized by information dependence—or the
234	need to learn information from their counterpart (Murnighan et al., 1999; Schweitzer & Croson,
235	1999; Schweitzer & Hsee, 2002). This feature of negotiations makes deception a particular challenge.
236	For example, by lying about the most they are willing to pay, negotiators may be able to attain a
237	better outcome.
238	To curb the risk of being deceived, negotiators can ask key questions. Conversely, to curb the
239	temptation of engaging in deception, negotiators can prepare by considering their responses to any
240	challenging or complex questions they may be asked prior to a negotiation (Fisher & Ury, 1981;
241	Thompson & Leonardelli, 2004; Thompson et al., 2010; see Helmold et al., 2022, Malhotra &
242	Bazerman, 2007; Galinsky & Schweitzer, 2015). Indeed, well-prepared negotiators are more likely to
243	gather information—by knowing what to ask—and to consider what not to reveal—by preparing
244	responses to difficult questions (e.g., “How much did you make at your last job?”) (Fisher & Ury, 1981;
245	see also Helmold et al., 2022; Malhotra & Bazerman, 2007). In a different but related domain,
246	research has demonstrated that insurance fraud investigators who interviewed claimants gleaned
247	more critical information from non-client sources than they did from client meetings (Warren &
248	Schweitzer, 2018). Though analogous studies have not been conducted in negotiations, and
249	contextual factors are likely to moderate the results, negotiators may be able to gather critical
250	information as they prepare to negotiate—before and after they meet with their counterpart.
251	In general, by investing greater time and resources in preparation, negotiators will improve their
252	outcomes. Preparation can boost negotiator confidence prior to a negotiation and strengthen their
253	ability to react to the other party’s moves during a negotiation (Malhotra & Bazerman, 2007;
254	Thompson, 2015; Thompson et al., 2010). In most cases, the link between preparation and
255	negotiation performance is very positive. However, scholars have suggested that negotiators can
256	overprepare for a negotiation in some cases (Thompson et al., 2010).
257	Developing BATNA, Reservation Price, Aspiration Price, And ZOPA
258	While setting the stage for a negotiation, negotiators should develop their alternatives and
259	understand the price or offer at which they would ultimately walk away (i.e., “reservation price”), as
260	well as the best outcome to which they aspire (i.e., “aspiration price”). They should also gain insight
261	into their counterpart’s alternatives and reservation price. Doing so can inform the offers they
262	make and give negotiators greater confidence during the communicating phase.
263	Best alternative to a negotiated agreement (batna)
264	Having an attractive option outside the current negotiation is the strongest source of power a
265	negotiating party can have (Fisher & Ury, 1981; Fisher et al., 2011). Research shows that negotiators
266	with a strong (vs. weak) BATNA are more likely to set favorable aspiration prices, make assertive
267	first offers, and ultimately attain better outcomes (Anderson & Galinsky, 2006; Buelens & Van
268	Poucke, 2004; Kagel et al., 1996; Magee et al., 2007; Pinkley et al., 1994; Lewicki et al., 2011; Wolfe &
269	Valley, 2001; see Fisher & Ury, 1981). This work suggests that one of the most important things
270	negotiators can do as they prepare to negotiate is to develop attractive alternatives. Yet little
271	research has investigated this topic directly.
272	Several studies have documented a robust relationship between having a strong BATNA and
273	obtaining favorable deal terms. A few studies, however, have deepened—and qualified—our
274	understanding of the relationship between BATNAs and negotiation performance. Specifically,
275	scholars have contrasted the effects of giving participants an explicit, weak BATNA with giving
276	participants no information about a BATNA whatsoever (“No BATNA,” though in practice there is
277	always some alternative to a failed negotiation). This work has found that “No BATNA” may be
278	preferable to a weak BATNA, because a weak BATNA can cause negotiators to set low aspirations
279	and focus their attention on their less desirable alternative (Schaerer et al., 2015). In addition,
280	uncertain BATNAs may have their own benefits (Pinkley et al., 2019). For example, negotiators with
281	uncertain BATNAs may feel optimistic and negotiate just as assertively as those with strong
282	BATNAs. In fact, when negotiators have no BATNA at all, merely imagining a strong BATNA can be
283	beneficial (Schaerer et al., 2018); this is because when negotiators imagine having an attractive
284	alternative (Schaerer et al., 2018), or when they have had an attractive alternative option in the past
285	(Brady et al., 2021), they may negotiate better deal terms.
286	Reservation and aspiration price
287	Though some prior work has conflated BATNA with reservation price—the price or offer at which a
288	negotiator would actually walk away from a deal—the two are conceptually distinct (Buelens & Van
289	Poucke, 2004). For example, because of pride, a sense of fairness, or inflated expectations, a
290	negotiator may exit a deal even when their counterpart is willing to give them a better outcome
291	than their BATNA. In contrast, a negotiator may be willing to accept a deal that is less favorable
292	than their BATNA if they care about their relational outcomes with the other party (or if they make
293	a mistake). Behavior in the Ultimatum game in which people reject positive sums of money—only to
294	receive $0—is consistent with this conceptual distinction (Güth et al., 1982; Pillutla & Murnighan,
295	1996). That is, a negotiator’s reservation price—also termed “resistance point” or “walkaway value”—
296	may be distinct from their BATNA.
297	Scholars have argued that negotiators should identify their reservation price before entering a
298	negotiation (Pruitt & Carnevale, 1993). Technically, this is the point at which the party is indifferent
299	to a deal or no deal. For example, a buyer should know the most that they would be willing to pay,
300	whereas the seller should know the least that they would be willing to accept. Adhering to
301	predetermined limits, however, is difficult. Related scholarship studying auction behavior has
302	found that when an auction is underway, people’s emotions tend to influence their behavior,
303	resulting in the negotiator disregarding limits they might have previously set and instead falling
304	prey to “competitive arousal” (Malhotra, 2010). Analogously, negotiators may be influenced by
305	emotion or competitive arousal and either walk away or fail to walk away from a negotiation,
306	ultimately attaining an outcome worse than their BATNA.
307	Another value negotiators should identify as they prepare for a negotiation is their aspiration price
308	or “target value” (Blount et al., 1995; Blount et al., 1996; White & Neale, 1994). This is the outcome
309	negotiators hope to achieve in their negotiation. Scholars suggest that negotiators should set
310	ambitious yet realistic aspirations (Fisher et al., 2011). Negotiators who set high aspiration prices
311	tend to be more successful in negotiations because a high aspiration price motivates assertive
312	behaviors (e.g., more haggling) and minimizes susceptibility to influence from the other party (see
313	Fisher et al., 2011; Siegel & Fouraker, 1960; Thompson, 2015). In some prior work, scholars have used
314	the initial prices negotiators propose to assess their aspirations (see O’Connor & Carnevale, 1997;
315	Pruitt & Lewis, 1975). In most articles, however, scholars have simply asked people to report their
316	aspirations.
317	Zone of possible agreement
318	The zone of possible agreement (ZOPA) is the difference between a buyer’s reservation price and a
319	seller’s reservation price (see Figure 2; also known as the “bargaining zone;” Shell, 2006; and
320	“bargaining surplus;” Raiffa, 1982; Farber & Katz, 1979; McKersie et al., 1965). The ZOPA includes the
321	set of possible deals that are acceptable to both parties. To determine the ZOPA in a negotiation,
322	negotiators need to identify two values: their own reservation price and their counterpart’s
323	reservation price. Both values may involve a degree of uncertainty and require effort to calculate;
324	however, it is particularly challenging to identify a counterpart’s reservation price, as people do not
325	usually reveal their reservation price in a negotiation. Negotiators simply hope to obtain a better
326	deal than their bottom line, so people must do their best to estimate the size of the ZOPA based on
327	the information they are able to obtain.
328	Figure 2: Zone of Possible Agreement
329	Note: In a distributive negotiation (e.g., a buyer and seller negotiating over the price of a used
330	car), the most a buyer can pay is the Buyer’s Reservation Point and the least a seller can accept is
331	the Seller’s Reservation Point. The zone between these points represents the Zone of Possible
332	Agreement (ZOPA); any amount within this zone indicates a possible deal. When deciding to
333	make a first offer, buyers are unlikely to know the Seller’s Reservation Point. Instead, they may
334	make an offer below the Seller’s Reservation Point, which could risk upsetting the seller or result
335	in an impasse; or, they may make an offer above the Seller’s Reservation Point, which could be
336	costly in terms of forgoing value.
337	Setting Goals
338	Goal setting, or the process of identifying and targeting a specific outcome, can benefit negotiators
339	prior to the negotiation. When a negotiator’s goal is to attain a specific price or deal, this goal reflects
340	their aspirations. Goals, however, can be broader than aspirations—and this is especially relevant in
341	negotiations with multiple rounds. For example, a negotiator may set a unique goal for each meeting
342	instead of working toward a consistent aspiration price in every interaction. In an initial meeting,
343	for instance, a negotiator may decide to build a long-term relationship, learn about their
344	counterpart’s underlying interests, or try to convince their counterpart that they will definitely go
345	to court. This same negotiator may adopt a new goal in each subsequent meeting.
346	Most studies investigating goals in the context of a negotiation have conceptualized goals as
347	aspirations. This work has found that specific, challenging goals tend to improve negotiated
348	outcomes (Lewicki et al., 2011; Stevens et al., 1993). Like studies that have identified a close link
349	between goal setting and motivation across many domains, negotiation scholars have found that
350	those who set specific and challenging goals tend to achieve better negotiation outcomes (Huber &
351	Neale, 1987; Neale & Bazerman, 1985; Northcraft et al., 1994; see Zetik & Stuhlmacher, 2002).
352	There are many open questions about the relationship between goal setting and negotiation. For
353	example, how should negotiators set goals? And how might they reset goals as they learn new
354	information during a negotiation? Scholarship has distinguished among different types of goals and
355	different types of negotiation contexts. Some of this work has distinguished between “Distributive
356	Negotiations” (i.e., negotiations characterized by a single issue, such as price) and “Integrative
357	Negotiations” (i.e., negotiations characterized by multiple issues in which tradeoffs are possible)
358	(Pruitt, 1981) (see Table 1). In distributive negotiations, one party’s gain comes at the other party’s
359	expense; in these cases, assertive goals can help negotiators claim a larger share of the so-called pie.
360	Conversely, in integrative negotiations, parties can achieve mutually beneficial outcomes by trading
361	off concessions across different issues or finding common interests (Neale & Bazerman, 1992; Fisher
362	et al., 1981; Rubin & Pruitt, 1994; Thompson et al., 2010); depending on the context, goal setting may
363	or may not promote integrative outcomes.
364	In related goal setting scholarship, researchers have found that performance goals, or goals that
365	focus on achievement or a specific outcome (Locke & Latham, 1990), boost performance in
366	distributive negotiations (Galinsky & Mussweiler, 2001), though they can also lead to greater
367	impasse rates and less integrative outcomes (Tasa et al., 2013). In contrast, learning goals, or goals
368	that focus on learning effective strategies by increasing one’s knowledge (Locke & Latham, 1990),
369	may be beneficial in integrative negotiations or multi-issue negotiations (Seijts & Latham, 2005). For
370	example, learning goals can help a negotiator gain knowledge about the other party’s interests and
371	allow for more creative solutions (Tasa et al., 2013). Learning goals are also beneficial for
372	interdependent tasks, or those in which one’s reputation could be impacted (Tinsley et al., 2002).
373	Though goal setting is a foundational construct in motivation, we know relatively little about the
374	goal setting process in negotiations (Locke & Lathan, 2002; Schweitzer et al., 2004); the majority of
375	scholarship investigating goal setting in negotiations has been completed in the lab, and as a result,
376	we know very little about how people set goals in relation to their identities, values, past
377	experiences, and broader objectives (Zetik & Stuhlmacher, 2002).
378	Perspective-Taking Of The Opposing Party
379	Perspective-taking is particularly important in negotiations. By understanding their counterpart’s
380	interests and reservation values, negotiators can attain far better outcomes for themselves (Fisher et
381	al., 2011; Thompson, 1990; Thompson & Hastie, 1990). However, understanding one’s own values is
382	difficult, and developing accurate beliefs about others’ values and interests is especially challenging
383	(De Dreu & Carnevale, 2003; Jervis, 1976; Ross & Ward, 1995; Thompson & Hrebec, 1996).
384	If negotiators are uncertain about their counterpart, or if they hold inaccurate beliefs about their
385	counterpart, they may misattribute the other party’s motives (Morris et al., 1999). For example, an
386	overly suspicious negotiator may assume their counterpart is asking them questions to identify
387	information that they can use to exploit them. Ultimately, negotiators who hold mistaken beliefs
388	about their counterpart reach less efficient outcomes (Thompson & Hrebec, 1996) or impasses
389	(Thompson, 1990). Thus, during the preparation phase, negotiators should spend time gathering
390	information and accurately determining the opposing party’s interests, priorities, and BATNA
391	(Galinsky & Mussweiler, 2001).
392	To do this optimally, negotiators should take the opposing party’s perspective. This is known as
393	perspective-taking, and it indicates a person’s capacity to consider the world from another’s point of
394	view and anticipate that party’s reaction to events (Davis, 1983; Moore, 2005). In a negotiation
395	context, perspective-taking can help negotiators identify the underlying interests of opposing
396	parties. This can be advantageous in integrative negotiations by helping negotiators identify
397	creative solutions that yield greater individual and joint gains (Galinsky & Moskowitz, 2000;
398	Galinsky & Mussweiler, 2001; Galinsky et al., 2008; Galinsky & Moskowitz, 2000; Neale & Bazerman,
399	1992; Lax & Sebenius, 1986). Perspective-taking is also advantageous in distributive negotiations, as
400	it can help negotiators avoid the power effect of an opponent’s first offer (Galinsky & Mussweiler,
401	2001) and instead elicit concessions (Neale & Bazerman, 1983). In this way, perspective-taking is
402	critical in negotiations, yet we know relatively little about the antecedents and individual traits
403	that can help negotiators consider others’ perspectives.
404	Who Is Negotiating
405	When it comes to setting the stage for a negotiation, it is important to consider one’s counterpart.
406	This section highlights how people’s power and status, group differences, and the relationship
407	between counterparts can affect negotiations. It also examines negotiations among more than two
408	parties—i.e., group and multiparty negotiations.
409	Power and status
410	Negotiations are heavily influenced by how much power individual negotiators have in the
411	negotiation. Power is typically defined as the amount of control individuals have over valuable
412	resources; in negotiations, the term is defined as the extent to which a negotiator can influence the
413	final outcome (Galinsky et al., 2017). Implicit in this definition is the idea that power is relative. In
414	negotiations, however, power to reach or block an outcome may be shared across multiple parties.
415	There are many sources of power in a negotiation (French & Raven, 1959; see Boothby et al., 2023;
416	Galinsky et al., 2017; Schaerer et al., 2020). The most studied source of power is having a strong
417	BATNA (Fisher & Ury, 1981; see Galinsky et al., 2017; Schaerer et al., 2020). Scholars have typically
418	studied the effects of having a strong BATNA by giving participants in an experiment a stronger or
419	weaker BATNA. These studies have found that a strong BATNA confers power to a negotiator,
420	making them less dependent on the other party to achieve their goals (Galinsky et al., 2017; Pinkley
421	et al., 2019; Pinkley et al., 1994; Schaerer et al., 2016; Schaerer et al., 2015). Prior work finds that
422	negotiators with a strong BATNA set higher goals (Pinkley, 1995), behave more aggressively
423	(Galinsky et al., 2003; Gruenfeld et al., 2008), and achieve better outcomes (Komorita & Leung, 1985;
424	Pinkley et al., 1994). Important open questions remain, however, with respect to how negotiators
425	might recognize the importance of developing a stronger BATNA—and then develop a stronger
426	BATNA as they prepare for a negotiation.
427	That said, in most negotiations, there are other sources of power beyond having a strong BATNA.
428	First, power can come from the amount of information a negotiator holds (see Galinksy et al., 2017;
429	Schaerer et al., 2020). Knowledge about each party’s underlying interests in a negotiation can help
430	negotiators claim value (Thompson & Hastie, 1990), and knowledge of one’s counterparts can
431	determine the most effective strategies to use in the negotiation (Brett, 2000; Pinkley, 1995; Wong,
432	2014).
433	Second, power can derive from status (see Galinksy et al., 2017; Schaerer et al., 2020). Status is the
434	extent to which someone is respected by another party (Brett & Thompson, 2016; Magee &
435	Galinsky, 2008), and it affords power for several reasons. First, high-status negotiators are viewed as
436	more competent than low-status negotiators (Rivera, 2012; 2015); second, they are also considered
437	more trustworthy (and deferred to more often) (Berger et al., 1972; Sauder et al., 2012), receive more
438	generous offers and greater compensation (Ball & Eckel, 1996; Belliveau et al., 1996), and create more
439	value (Blader & Chen, 2012).
440	Third, power can come from social capital (see Galinsky et al., 2017; Schaerer et al., 2020). Social
441	capital—or establishing and maintaining a strong network and connections (Kilduff & Brass, 2010)—
442	allows negotiators to secure better opportunities and negotiate better deals, affording greater access
443	to negotiation partners and coalitions (Kim & Fragale, 2005; Kravitz & Iwanisek, 1984). According to
444	Schaerer and colleagues (2020), power can also come from a person’s expertise and their ability to
445	coerce others into compliance.
446	Turning to consequences of power, several scholars have demonstrated that negotiators with more
447	power attain more favorable outcomes (Gunia et al., 2013; Schaerer et al., 2015). Not only do
448	negotiators with greater power have more leverage in a negotiation, but these negotiators also
449	derive psychic benefits—allowing negotiators to feel powerful—that help them attain better
450	outcomes (Keltner et al., 2003; Galinsky et al., 2015; Galinsky et al., 2017). For example, high-power
451	negotiators feel more confident than those with less power (Fast et al., 2012; See et al., 2011; Tost et
452	al., 2012); they are also considered more optimistic (Anderson & Galinsky, 2006). Compared to
453	negotiators with less power, high-power negotiators are more persuasive (Kilduff & Galinsky, 2013;
454	Lammers et al., 2013; Schmid & Schmid Mast, 2013), better at seeing the bigger picture (Kifer et al.,
455	2013; Kraus et al., 2011; Magee et al., 2008; Smith & Trope, 2006), and less likely to be influenced by
456	their counterpart (Galinsky et al., 2008). When negotiators have greater power, they feel less
457	distressed toward others’ suffering (van Kleef et al., 2008), they experience less stress themselves
458	(Schmid & Schmid Mast, 2013), and they are less likely to be swayed by the other party’s tactics
459	(Schmid & Schmid Mast, 2013).
460	However, the consequences of power may depend on the source of power (see Galinsky et al., 2017;
461	Schaerer et al., 2020). Though favorable alternatives are a key source of power in negotiations
462	(Fisher & Ury, 1981; see Galinsky et al., 2017), these alternatives can also anchor the negotiator. For
463	example, negotiators with a weak BATNA may become anchored by their BATNA, and ultimately
464	claim less value than those with no BATNA at all (Schaerer et al., 2015). Similarly, negotiators with
465	multiple alternatives often become anchored by the mid-point of their alternatives (rather than the
466	best alternative) and end up claiming less value than those with one strong alternative (Schaerer et
467	al., 2016).
468	Scholarship has also considered relative levels of power within dyads (see Schaerer et al., 2020).
469	Some studies have found that dyads with equal-power negotiators create greater value than those
470	with unequal-power negotiators (Giebels et al., 2000; Mannix & Neale, 1993). Other studies,
471	however, have found that relative power within a dyad does not influence the efficiency of
472	outcomes (Lawler & Yoon, 1993; Wiltermuth et al., 2018) and that unequal power within a dyad
473	helps negotiators create value (Greer & van Kleef, 2010). Possibly, factors beyond the distribution of
474	power can moderate how efficiently negotiators structure agreements (see Schaerer et al., 2020).
475	High-power negotiators can act powerful by enacting behaviors that help them attain more
476	favorable outcomes. For example, high-power negotiators are not only more likely to make a first
477	offer than their low-power counterparts (Blader & Chen, 2012; Magee et al., 2007), but they are also
478	more likely to make an ambitious first offer (Magee et al., 2007; Schaerer et al., 2020). In addition,
479	high-power negotiators are more likely to ask for more (Babcock & Laschever, 2003; Magee et al.,
480	2007), less likely to make concessions, and more likely to retaliate when the other party expresses
481	anger (van Kleef & Côté, 2007; van Kleef et al., 2006).
482	Negotiation scholarship has identified specific behaviors that may afford negotiators power or
483	status. Common behaviors include expressing dominance (Kim et al., 2006; Mast & Hall, 2003);
484	dominance is known to project power (Bacharach & Lawler, 1981; Burgoon & Dunbar, 2006; Dunbar,
485	2004; Carnevale et al., 1981), eliciting concessions from the other party (Bacharach & Lawler, 1981;
486	Camras, 1984; Komorita & Brenner, 1968; Pruitt, 1981; Rosa & Mazur, 1979; Sinaceur & Tiedens,
487	2006), and enabling negotiators to claim greater value (Camras, 1984; Sinaceur & Tidens, 2006;
488	Sinaceur et al., 2011). For example, negotiators can exhibit dominance by staring at their
489	counterpart (Lewis & Fry, 1977), taking an aggressive tone (Komorita & Brenner, 1968), or expressing
490	anger (Sinaceur & Tiedens, 2006). Negotiators may also use subtle displays of dominance such as
491	adopting a powerful stance, taking up extensive space with their posture (Huang et al., 2011;
492	Tiedens & Fragale, 2003), or interrupting the other party (Mast & Hall, 2003).
493	Dominance behaviors may benefit negotiators differently depending on the level of power that
494	they hold in the negotiation. Specifically, research shows that lower-power negotiators who were
495	instructed to behave dominantly (vs. those who were not) were better able to claim value because
496	displays of dominance made them feel more powerful, leading to more assertive behavior
497	(Wiltermuth et al., 2018). Additionally, examining dominance at the dyadic level suggests that there
498	are coordination benefits to such displays: Dyads in which the more powerful negotiator acted
499	dominantly and the other did not created more value than dyads in which neither, both, or only the
500	lower-power negotiator used dominance displays (Wiltermuth et al., 2018). This research finds that
501	if one party’s dominant behavior elicits submissiveness in the other party, mutually beneficial
502	outcomes may ensue by prompting a greater information exchange that leads to increased value
503	creation (Wiltermuth et al., 2015; Wiltermuth et al., 2018).
504	Dominance behaviors, particularly anger expressions, may benefit negotiators differently
505	depending on the person and the expression itself. Though anger expressions convey dominance
506	(Belkin et al., 2013) and signal power (Frijda, 1986; Tiedens, 2001) and status (Brescoll & Uhlmann,
507	2008; Tiedens, 2001), research shows that only men were afforded status when expressing anger
508	(Brescoll & Uhlmann, 2008). Additionally, low-intensity anger expressions led to a boost in status
509	over sadness or neutral expressions, yet high-intensity anger expressions did not—because they
510	yield lower perceptions of competence and warmth (Gaertig et al., 2019).
511	Negotiators may engage in other behaviors to show or attain power and status. Powerful
512	negotiators may be successful in negotiations because they can coerce their counterpart into
513	compliance by punishing (De Dreu, 1995) or threatening (Sinaceur et al., 2011; Wiltermuth et al.,
514	2018; Wiltermuth et al., 2015) them. Alternatively, some research also suggests that “warmth”
515	behaviors (Anderson & Kilduff, 2009; Flynn et al., 2006), or showing concern for the welfare of
516	others (Hardy & Van Vugt, 2006; Willer, 2009), can afford higher status. However, open questions
517	remain with respect to the contextual and individual difference moderators that enable people to
518	attain and project power.
519	Relationships
520	Negotiation occurs among strangers, acquaintances, work colleagues, and close relational friends or
521	partners. In many cases, negotiators are interdependent (Cross & Madson, 1997; Kashima et al., 1995).
522	They may feel more or less connected to the other party depending on their shared history,
523	individual or group differences, and culture (Gelfand et al., 2006). For example, women typically feel
524	more connected to their negotiation partner than men (Amanatullah et al., 2008; Bowles et al.,
525	2007).
526	Negotiating with a familiar counterpart versus a stranger or acquaintance does not ensure a better
527	outcome (Greenhalgh & Chapman, 1998; Thompson & DeHarpport, 1998; see McGinn, 2006). In fact,
528	several studies show that negotiating with a close other, or having strong relational goals in a
529	negotiation, can lead to a greater willingness to compromise—causing negotiators to make more
530	generous offers, claim less value, and become more willing to accept a suboptimal agreement
531	(Amanatullah et al., 2008; Curhan et al., 2008; Fry et al., 1983; Halpern, 1994; 1997; Howard et al.,
532	2007; Jones & Rachlin, 2006; Patton & Balakrishnan, 2010; Ten Velden et al., 2009). Scholars have
533	cited “relational accommodation,” or a willingness to sacrifice economic outcomes to bolster or
534	maintain relational outcomes (Curhan et al., 2008). That is, negotiators may worry about harming
535	their relationship with the other party if they act aggressively or use distributive tactics
536	(Amanatullah & Morris, 2010; Babcock et al., 2006; Bowles et al., 2007; Bear & Segel-Karpas, 2015;
537	Curhan et al., 2008; Patton & Balakrishnan, 2010). It is possible, however, that prior scholarship—
538	which has largely ignored post-negotiation behavior and long-term relationships—has
539	mischaracterized relational accommodation as an error. In line with scholarship documenting the
540	economic value of post-negotiation behavior (see Hart & Schweitzer, 2022), relational
541	accommodation may not only promote relational outcomes, but also boost long-term economic
542	outcomes.
543	The expectations people develop when they negotiate with familiar counterparts represent a
544	related challenge. When negotiating with a familiar counterpart, people may expect their partner
545	to be friendly and cooperative (Patton & Balakrishnan, 2010; Ramirez-Fernandez et al., 2018), or to
546	make more generous offers (Ramirez-Fernandez et al., 2018). If these expectations go unmet,
547	negotiators are more likely to negatively evaluate their counterparts and resist reaching an
548	agreement. Perspective-taking, however, can mitigate this problem, as long as negotiators realize
549	they have inflated expectations of their relational partners (Ramirez-Fernandez et al., 2018).
550	Group differences
551	Group differences such as gender, race, and culture can influence negotiation behavior and
552	outcomes. In some cases, individuals may act differently based on group differences. For example,
553	women may be less likely to initiate a negotiation than men (Kugler et al., 2018). In other cases,
554	negotiators are treated differently based on group differences; for example, buyers who are Black
555	may be offered higher sales prices than buyers who are White (Ayres & Siegelman, 1995). In
556	addition, people may be evaluated differently, even when they behave similarly. For example,
557	women who act assertively may be perceived less favorably than assertive men (Amanatullah &
558	Tinsley, 2013). Ultimately, the manner in which people are treated and evaluated can influence how
559	they behave. This section focuses on how group differences influence negotiations.
560	Substantial literature has investigated gender differences in negotiation (see Bowles et al., 2022;
561	Toosi et al., 2020). Some of the earliest work investigating gender differences explored the idea that
562	women behave more cooperatively than men (Rubin & Brown, 2013), but scholars have found
563	conflicting evidence in support of this thesis (see Kray & Thompson, 2004; Rubin & Brown, 2013;
564	Walters et al., 1998). It is quite possible that gender differences themselves may have changed over
565	the past 50 years; replications of studies conducted several decades ago may yield different results
566	because the phenomena have changed. Though negotiation scholarship has focused more on the
567	challenges women face in negotiations, each of the two dominant genders experience unique
568	challenges in negotiation (Mazei et al., 2022).
569	The decision to initiate a negotiation is particularly important, and several scholars have identified a
570	consistent pattern: Women are less likely to initiate a negotiation than men (Kugler et al., 2018;
571	Small et al., 2007). In a classic study, an experimenter describes a pay range for performance,
572	compliments the participant for performing well, and then offers the participant the lowest end of
573	the pay range. In these studies, women are less likely to ask for more money than men (Small et al.,
574	2007). More broadly, women are less likely to initiate negotiations, even when negotiations are
575	consequential, as is the case in job negotiations (Babcock & Laschever, 2003; Amanatullah & Tinsley,
576	2013; Artz et al., 2018). When women do negotiate, they may attain worse outcomes than men
577	(Bowles et al., 2005; see Mazei et al., 2015).
578	However, many gender effects vary by context. Often, negotiation studies involve masculine-
579	stereotyped domains (Small et al., 2007; Kugler et al., 2018; see Bowles et al., 2022). For example,
580	although women are less likely to negotiate their salaries than men (Babcock & Laschever, 2003;
581	Bowles et al., 2007; Kugler et al., 2018; Leibbrandt & List, 2015; Mazei et al., 2015), women are just as
582	likely to negotiate—and to do so assertively—when the negotiation involves workload or family-
583	friendly workplace practices (Bear, 2011; Berdahl & Moon, 2013; Bowles et al., 2019; Rousseau et al.,
584	2006; Rudman & Mescher, 2013).
585	Gendered norms and expectations may influence how men and women negotiate. In the United
586	States, women are stereotypically more collectivistic, agreeable, and cooperative than men, who are
587	stereotypically more individualistic, assertive, and competitive (Cuddy et al., 2015; Kray et al., 2001).
588	People may internalize gender stereotypes and behave in accordance with their gender
589	expectations (Eagly & Wood, 2012; Kray et al., 2001; Kray et al., 2002; Eagly & Wood, 2012). In
590	negotiations, gendered stereotypes may result in beliefs that women do not negotiate assertively or
591	at all (Bowles et al., 2007; Kray et al., 2001; Kray et al., 2002). Exposure to such stereotypes may not
592	only hinder women’s intentions to negotiate, but also adversely affect women who do negotiate. For
593	example, people report that they are more willing to work with men who negotiate than with
594	women who negotiate (Amanatullah & Tinsley, 2013; Bowles et al., 2007; Duguid & Thomas-Hunt,
595	2015); they also ascribe more negative attributions to women who negotiate (e.g., women who
596	negotiate are more immodest or materialistic) (Amanatullah & Tinsley, 2013; Al Dabbagh et al., 2016;
597	Artz et al., 2018).
598	Gender differences in negotiations are most pronounced when gender stereotypes are salient
599	(Bowles et al., 2004; Kugler et al., 2018; Kray & Gelfand, 2009; Mazei et al., 2015; see Bowles et al.,
600	2022). Contextual features, including the work setting and culture can cue gender stereotypes (Kolb
601	& McGinn, 2009; Tost, 2015; Galinsky et al., 2018; see Bowles et al., 2022), which can exacerbate
602	gender differences (see Kugler et al., 2018; Mazei et al., 2015). For example, in male-stereotyped
603	settings (e.g., selling motorcycle parts) men are more likely to initiate a negotiation and to negotiate
604	better outcomes than women (Galinsky et al., 2003; Kolb & McGinn, 2009; Roth, 2009; Small et al.,
605	2007; Sturm, 2009; Kugler et al., 2018; Bear & Babcock, 2012; Mazei et al., 2015). Recent work has
606	found that gender effects can be diminished when negotiators learn about their counterparts and
607	perceive them as individuals, rather than as representations of a social group (see Bowles et al.,
608	2022).
609	To address gender differences and increase the likelihood that women will initiate negotiations, some
610	scholars have proposed that women reframe the negotiation process. Specifically, women may be
611	more likely to initiate a negotiation when they view the context as an opportunity to ask for
612	something, rather than an opportunity to negotiate (Small et al., 2007). Opportunities to make a
613	request are viewed as more polite than opportunities for negotiation, and thus, they are more
614	congruent with stereotypical gender roles.
615	Advocacy also affects how women perform in negotiations. Women are much less likely than men
616	to advocate for themselves in negotiations, in part because they face a higher risk when they do so
617	(Amanatullah & Morris, 2010; Bowles et al., 2022). However, when women advocate for others in a
618	negotiation, they are perceived as more assertive and more effective (Amanatullah & Morris, 2010;
619	Bowles et al., 2022; Mazei et al., 2015). This is consistent with gender stereotypes that perceive
620	women as more communal than men, and with those that view women more positively when they
621	advocate for others versus themselves (Amanatullah & Tinsley, 2013).
622	One strategy for improving women’s success in negotiations is to directly address the inequality in
623	outcomes. By informing women that men reach more successful outcomes in negotiation before the
624	negotiation process begins, women can act more assertively and work more strategically to attain
625	better outcomes (Kray et al., 2001). Similarly, by decreasing ambiguity around the scope and
626	standard for agreement in a negotiation, both parties can reduce any gender differences in
627	negotiated outcomes (Bowles et al., 2005; see Bowles et al., 2022). Interestingly, priming women with
628	power can further mitigate gender differences (Hong & van der Wijst, 2013; Galinsky et al., 2013;
629	Small et al., 2007), as some scholars have conceptualized gender differences as power differences
630	(Galinsky & Schweitzer, 2015).
631	A few studies have documented gender differences in negotiation behavior. Specifically, prior
632	research has found that women are more likely to change their strategy based on who the other
633	party is—for example, by compromising more when negotiating with other women (Bowles &
634	Flynn, 2010; Curhan et al., 2008; Miles & LaSalle, 2009), by exhibiting more conflict-avoidant
635	behaviors, and by acting more ethically than men (Kennedy et al., 2017; Kray & Haselhuhn, 2012;
636	Pierce & Thompson, 2018). Simultaneously, women are more likely to be deceptive when advocating
637	for others versus themselves (thus, engaging in the same level of deception as men) (Kouchaki &
638	Kray, 2018).
639	Research also suggests that both men and women adjust their negotiation strategies depending on
640	the gender of the other party. When negotiating with women, both men and women tend to be
641	more deceptive—possibly because women are perceived as less competent and more agreeable than
642	men (Kray et al., 2014). Conversely, when negotiating with men, people, in general, are less trusting
643	of men’s initial offers (Maoz, 2009); they are also more likely to doubt men who claim that they
644	cannot make concessions (Bowles & Flynn, 2010)—perhaps because men are perceived as
645	hypercompetitive.
646	Scholars have also considered the influence of being a man in negotiations (Kennedy & Kray, 2015;
647	Mazei et al., 2021; Mazei et al., 2022). Like women, men also face unique pressures and barriers that
648	affect their behavior in negotiations. A key driver of men’s behavior in negotiations is the pressure
649	to demonstrate their ability, alongside a belief that negotiation is a “man’s job” (Haselhuhn et al.,
650	2014; Kray et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2017; Mazei et al., 2021). Based on work on precarious manhood—
651	the idea that men need to show their masculinity to keep their status as a “real man” (Vandello &
652	Bosson, 2013; Vandello et al., 2008)—underperformance in a negotiation may cause men to lose face
653	or status (Kennedy & Kray, 2015; Kray & Haselhuhn, 2012; Lee et al., 2017; see Mazei et al., 2021). As
654	a result, men may become more competitive (Netchaeva et al., 2015) or more likely to behave
655	unethically in negotiations (Haselhuhn et al., 2014; Kray et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2017).
656	In comparison to research on gender, less is known about how race and ethnicity influence the
657	negotiation process. Existing research on race and ethnicity in negotiation outcomes has
658	emphasized how stereotypes affect people’s behavior toward negotiators of different races and
659	ethnicities. This work has found that Black people attain worse outcomes in negotiations compared
660	to White people (Ayres, 1991; Ayres & Siegelman, 1995). This is likely due to racial stereotypes that
661	negatively characterize Black people (e.g., as incompetent; Devine, 1989; Devine & Elliot, 1995; Plous
662	& Williams, 1995). More recent work has directly examined this and found that race-based
663	expectations (e.g., “that Black people should not ask for more”; McConahay, 1983; Sidanius et al.,
664	2000) lead to worse outcomes for Black negotiators (Hernandez et al., 2019). Similar to women, Black
665	people are expected to negotiate less, and when this expectation is violated, outcomes worsen for
666	those negotiators.
667	Race-based expectations can also influence reactions to emotional expressions (Adam & Shirako,
668	2010; Salerno et al., 2019). For example, expressing anger, which can elicit concessions during a
669	negotiation (Sinaceur et al., 2011), is less beneficial for Black (vs. White) negotiators—and less
670	beneficial for women than for men—because the display of emotion is used to discredit Black and
671	women negotiators (Salerno et al., 2019). However, other research has found that East Asian
672	negotiators who express anger elicit greater cooperation than non-East-Asian negotiators who do
673	the same; this may be the result of the violation of stereotypic expectations (Adam & Shirako, 2010).
674	That is, because the anger expression is unexpected, it serves as a strong signaling value. Thus,
675	people’s expectations and stereotypes around race and ethnicity may affect how they perceive
676	others and negotiate.
677	Culture also plays a significant role in shaping both negotiation behavior and negotiated outcomes.
678	The cultural context has a strong influence on how people interpret behavior as it defines what is
679	appropriate during a negotiation (Brett et al., 2014; Brett, 2007; Gibson, 1999; Hall, 1976). Culture
680	affects what people attend to (Ambady et al., 1996; Gelfand et al., 2001; Gunia et al., 2016), what they
681	expect (Brett et al., 2014), and how they believe they should behave (Aslani et al., 2013; Aslani et al.,
682	2016; Brett et al., 2014). A few leading scholars have developed useful frameworks for
683	understanding the influence of culture on negotiation.
684	Much of the research on culture has compared negotiation behavior and outcomes of people from
685	two or more nations or cultural groups, with an emphasis on differences between East and West
686	cultures (Gunia et al., 2016). For example, researchers have theorized that Eastern and Middle
687	Eastern cultures place a greater focus on relational outcomes (Aslani et al., 2013; Gelfand et al., 2012),
688	use more persuasion and offer-making strategies (vs. information exchange strategies) (Gunia et al.,
689	2011; Liu & Wilson, 2011; Lügger et al., 2015), and prefer less direct confrontation (Adam et al., 2010;
690	Brett et al., 2014; Oetzel & Ting-Toomey, 2003; Semnani-Azad & Adair, 2013).
691	Emerging research has moved beyond the East-versus-West paradigm. For example, Lu (2023)
692	suggests that findings showing that Asian people have higher starting salaries than White people
693	conflates three groups of Asians: East Asians, Southeast Asians, and South Asians. When we
694	disentangle these different Asian populations, we find that South Asians earn the highest salaries of
695	all ethnicities, but that East Asians and Southeast Asians earn some of the lowest.
696	Another important framework for understanding negotiation behavior and outcomes categorizes
697	cultures into dignity, face, and honor cultures. These categories can account for different conflict
698	styles and explain how people construe behavior and approach reconciliation (Aslani et al., 2013).
699	Specifically, in dignity cultures (e.g., most Western European and North American cultures), a
700	person’s self-worth is intrinsic, and the distribution of power is egalitarian; in these cultures, people
