700	person’s self-worth is intrinsic, and the distribution of power is egalitarian; in these cultures, people
701	negotiate directly and rationally. In face cultures (e.g., many East and Southeast Asian cultures), a
702	person’s self-worth is derived from their social interactions, and power is derived from a stable
703	hierarchy; in these cultures, people negotiate less directly, value humility, and seek to fulfill their
704	collective duty. In honor cultures (e.g., many Middle Eastern and Latin American cultures), a
705	person’s self-worth is a function of how they are viewed by society, and power is hierarchical,
706	dynamic, and often contested; in these cultures, people use both direct and indirect strategies to
707	negotiate and are highly emotionally expressive. Research suggests that negotiators from honor and
708	face cultures use more competitive strategies during a negotiation than those from dignity cultures
709	(Aslani et al., 2016). Negotiators from honor and face cultures may also claim more value than their
710	dignity culture counterparts, leading to greater distributive tactics such as feigned anger,
711	exaggeration, and pressure (Leung & Cohen, 2011; Aslani et al., 2016, Yao et al., 2017). In contrast,
712	negotiators from dignity cultures tend to engage in more integrative strategies by sharing
713	information and focusing on joint gains.
714	Though researchers have made important strides in developing our understanding of the effects of
715	gender, race, and culture in negotiations, there is a need for new research. First, the influence of
716	gender, race, and culture are likely to be important, but they may shift over time. For example,
717	attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors toward gender differences documented in the 20th century may
718	not reflect attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors today. Moreover, the existing literature has focused
719	exclusively on men and women—leaving many open questions about negotiations for people with
720	non-binary gender identities (or those beyond the man/woman dichotomy).
721	Second, future work should investigate the intersection of these variables (Shan et al., 2019), as
722	stereotypes and gender norms may differ across races and cultures (Ghavami & Peplau, 2013;
723	Rosette et al., 2016; Phelan & Rudman, 2010). Similarly, stereotypes may differ across cultures for
724	men and women. For example, White men may be viewed as assertive, whereas Asian men may be
725	viewed as shy (Ghavami & Peplau, 2013). Similarly, Black women may be stereotyped differently
726	than White women (Purdie-Vaughns & Eibach, 2008; Rosette et al., 2016; Sturm, 2009). In addition,
727	status tends to vary across gender, race, and culture (Berger et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2005)—often in
728	ways that influence how people are treated in negotiations. For example, prior work has found that
729	White men are offered lower prices when buying a car than women or Black people (Ayres &
730	Siegelman, 1995), and that Black jobseekers are offered lower starting salaries than White
731	jobseekers (Hernandez et al., 2019). These findings suggest that additional work is needed to explore
732	intersections between race and gender (Bowles et al., 2022; Clair et al., 2019; Toosi et al., 2020). In
733	addition, future work should examine other group differences, such as those based on sexual
734	identity (Hudson & Ghani, 2021).
735	Group and multiparty negotiations
736	Not all negotiations occur between two parties; rather, negotiations commonly take place within
737	larger groups or between teams. Team negotiations are common and far more complex than one-on-
738	one negotiations (Brodt & Thompson, 2001; Thompson et al., 1996; Polzer et al., 1995; see Boothby et
739	al., 2023; Cohen & Thompson, 2011). A few studies have investigated team negotiations and found
740	that teams generally outperform individuals by claiming more value and achieving greater joint
741	gains than individual negotiators (Brodt & Thompson, 2001; Cohen et al., 2014; Huffmeier et al.,
742	2019; Morgan & Tindale, 2002; Polzer, 1996; Thompson et al., 1996; see Cohen & Thompson, 2011 for
743	a review). In contrast to individual negotiators, teams process information more efficiently and
744	solve problems more effectively (De Dreu, 2010). For example, compared to individual negotiators,
745	negotiating teams are more likely to identify compatible issues and attain mutually beneficial
746	tradeoffs (Huffmeier et al., 2019; Morgan & Tindale, 2002; Polzer, 1996; Thompson et al., 1996).
747	There are several possible reasons why teams outperform individuals. First, in contrast to solo
748	negotiators, some members of a negotiation team are less likely to focus their attention on what
749	they need to say next, and instead focus their attention on their counterparts. Second, teams tend to
750	exchange more information than individuals (Cohen et al., 2014; Thompson et al., 1996), and are
751	more likely to identify optimal outcomes (Cohen et al., 2014). Teams are also more likely to have a
752	skilled negotiator, such as someone who asks effective questions and gleans valuable information
753	from their counterpart (Huffmeier et al., 2019).
754	Scholars have also identified some disadvantages to team negotiation. For example, some research
755	shows that teams generate worse relational outcomes than individual negotiators (Huffmeier et al.,
756	2019); this may reflect the fact that teams are more competitive (Naquin & Kurtzberg, 2009; Polzer,
757	1996). Ultimately, compared to individuals, negotiating parties are less trusting of teams (Swaab et
758	al., 2021). Swaab et al. (2021) offers a prescription: When negotiating as a team, members should
759	engage in pre-negotiation conversations, identify superordinate goals, and be mindful of the need to
760	develop trust.
761	Multiparty negotiations involve three or more parties (see Crump & Glendon, 2003). With multiple
762	parties, negotiators need to gather and process information more efficiently, and potentially be
763	more judicious in how they reveal information. Compared to dyadic negotiations, multiparty
764	negotiations are significantly more complex (see Table 1).
765	Individuals in multiparty negotiations may also feel they have less control over outcomes than
766	those in dyadic negotiations (Kerr, 1989; Kramer, 1991); as a result, they may expect less reciprocity.
767	For example, a negotiator could make a deal with one party and leave another party (or several
768	parties) out of an agreement. The mere prospect of being left out of a deal may drive negotiator
769	behavior, such as a desire to form coalitions (Moreland, 2010).
770	In this way, multiparty negotiations are more challenging—and more likely to end in an impasse—
771	than dyadic negotiations (Traavik, 2011). One interesting feature of multiparty negotiations is that
772	negotiators are likely to find allies, at least among some counterparts, with regard to certain issues
773	(Raiffa, 1982). Reflecting the complexity of multiparty negotiation, research shows that multiparty
774	negotiators have weaker fixed-pie perceptions and engage in more integrative strategies than
775	dyadic negotiators (Kern et al., 2020).
776	Every human group, across cultures and throughout history, is characterized by hierarchy
777	(Galinsky & Schweitzer, 2015). This means that some members of a group have greater power than
778	others. The study of hierarchy in negotiations, especially hierarchy within a negotiation team,
779	represents a significant opportunity for future scholarship. Doyle and colleagues (2023) suggest that
780	hierarchical structures within a team might be harmful to reaching efficient agreements, as
781	hierarchy reduces information elaboration and increases competitive behaviors. Hierarchy,
782	however, may also promote team functioning—by enabling team members to identify specific roles
783	and responsibilities. Possibly, hierarchical negotiating teams will outperform less hierarchical
784	negotiating teams.
785	Who is negotiating: conclusion
786	Negotiations are shaped by individuals and their power dynamics, as well as their relationships and
787	social identities. People often negotiate as part of a group or a team, rather than a dyad. Knowing
788	the other negotiating party (or parties) is an important part of setting the stage for a negotiation. A
789	growing literature has expanded our understanding of the negotiation process and negotiated
790	outcomes as they vary across these contexts, but there is still a great deal to explore in the future.
791	Identifying Issues
792	Scholars have classified types of issues in a negotiation. Distributive issues fall along a single
793	dimension (e.g., price, salary) and involve one party’s gain coming at the other’s expense (Pruitt,
794	1981). For example, if a buyer agrees to pay a high price, it is beneficial for the seller but harmful for
795	the buyer.
796	Integrative issues create opportunities for joint gains (Pruitt, 1981). Unlike distributive negotiations,
797	which are characterized by a single issue, integrative negotiations involve multiple issues (e.g., start
798	date, location, salary). Negotiators may value different outcomes across the issues (e.g., one party
799	may value a particular location, whereas the other party may place more emphasis on a particular
800	start date). In integrative negotiations, parties can structure agreements that create value. Notably,
801	in distributive negotiations, parties can create value simply by finding an agreement, whereas in
802	integrative negotiations, parties can create value by finding efficient tradeoffs across issues
803	(“expanding the pie”) and reaching integrative outcomes (Bazerman & Neale, 1982; Brett &
804	Thompson, 2016; Fisher et al., 2011; Kong et al., 2014; Patton, 2015; Pruitt & Rubin, 1986). For
805	example, in a job negotiation, a prospective employee may value where they work more than the
806	start date, whereas the hiring manager may prioritize the start date over the location. By making
807	trades across issues, negotiators can create value (Froman & Cohen, 1970). As a result, a negotiation
808	with many issues, or a negotiator who effectively identifies many issues, can extract substantial
809	value from an agreement.
810	To transform a distributive negotiation into an integrative negotiation, a vital step is to identify and
811	add additional issues to the negotiation (e.g., buying in bulk, changing the delivery time, etc.). The
812	ability to identify and add issues is a key skill for negotiators, yet the dominant roleplay paradigm
813	pre-identifies negotiation issues. Because this paradigm assigns people to either distributive or
814	integrative negotiations, our knowledge of how to recognize and propose additional issues—with
815	the goal of making negotiations more integrative—is limited. In turn, it is important to note that
816	even within integrative negotiations, there is a dominant, distributive dimension. That is, many
817	integrative negotiations retain a significant distributive component. For example, job or home
818	negotiations may involve multiple integrative issues, whereas salary and price are likely to be
819	dominant distributive issues.
820	Scholars have also identified compatible issues, for which both negotiating parties may want the
821	same outcome (also known as “common value issues”; Lax & Sebenius, 1986; Pruitt & Carnevale,
822	1993; Raiffa, 1982). For example, both the buyer and the seller of a home may want an early closing
823	date. Anticipating the potential for compatible issues is critical, as one party may mislead their
824	counterpart (O’Connor & Carnevale, 1993). For example, a seller who knows that the buyer would
825	like an early closing date may accommodate their counterpart in exchange for a higher price—even
826	when they too would prefer an early closing date (i.e., sandbagging).
827	A fourth type of issue is indifference, which indicates a lack of value for one of the negotiating
828	parties (Olekalns & Smith, 2007). These are issues that negotiators may introduce to create an
829	opportunity for concessions. For example, an employer may be indifferent to the rotations a new
830	employee completes first. However, by introducing the issue and asserting that they have a
831	preference (when, in reality, they do not), the employer may create an opportunity to extract a
832	concession.
833	Anticipating Questions And Preparing Responses
834	In negotiations, people may be asked questions that they do not want to answer (van Beest et al.,
835	2011; Steinel et al., 2009). To effectively prepare for a negotiation, negotiators should anticipate these
836	difficult questions (e.g., “Do you have other offers?” or “How much money did you make in your last
837	position?”). Strategies for doing this effectively (e.g., perspective-taking, roleplaying) have not been
838	investigated, though scholars have studied different responses to difficult questions. One option is to
839	simply decline to answer; however, people who take this approach—those who choose not to
840	respond to a direct question—may be viewed negatively (e.g., as less trustworthy or less likable)
841	(John et al., 2016). In addition, by refusing to answer a question, people still reveal information. For
842	example, in response to the question, “Do you have other offers?” a person who states, “I would
843	rather not answer” implicitly signals relevant information.
844	A second type of response involves deception (Gaspar & Schweitzer, 2013; Rogers et al., 2017). In
845	response to a difficult question, people may lie by commission (i.e., by explicitly presenting
846	something false as true). People may also lie by omission when they omit relevant information to
847	project a misleading impression. For example, a negotiation counterpart may assume that a
848	prospective candidate has other offers, and the prospective candidate may intentionally fail to
849	correct this impression. In general, people can improve their negotiation outcomes by lying as long
850	as the deception goes unnoticed. Once deception is detected, however, liars lose trust and suffer
851	both relational and economic costs (see DePaulo & Kashy, 1998; Rogers & Norton, 2011; Rogers et al.,
852	2017; Schweitzer et al., 2006).
853	A few studies have investigated alternatives to honesty and deception. One alternative involves
854	deflection, or responding to a counterpart with an entirely new question. For example, in response
855	to a question about how much they were paid in their last job, candidates may ask, “What is the
856	most you have paid someone in this position?” Deflection often shifts the conversation to a new
857	topic by violating and then cueing the conversation norm to answer a question (Bitterly &
858	Schweitzer, 2020). In many cases, naïve negotiators fail to return to their initial question and
859	instead follow the conversational flow of the deflection (Bitterly & Schweitzer, 2020). In this way,
860	deflecting unwanted questions can lead to beneficial negotiation outcomes, including more positive
861	evaluations (e.g., greater trust or liking) and less information revealed—without the risk of getting
862	caught trying to deceive the other person.
863	By preparing to ask and answer difficult questions, negotiators can strategically recognize deflection
864	and address complex topics with ease. In some cases, they can even practice their responses in
865	advance. Without preparation, however, and under time pressure, negotiators may answer difficult
866	questions—deceptively or honestly—in ways that they later regret.
867	Developing A Concession Plan
868	In most negotiations, people make concessions as they move closer to the other party’s interests
869	(Pruitt, 1981). Negotiators who develop a concession plan—by considering what first offers to make
870	and how to make subsequent concessions prior to the negotiation—are likely to outperform those
871	who do not. However, the lack of research investigating both concession plans and concession
872	patterns reflects fundamental gaps in our understanding of negotiations. It also highlights an
873	important opportunity for future scholarship.
874	We do know that concessions reveal information about negotiators’ interests (Weingart et al., 1990),
875	signal cooperation, and cue reciprocity (Thuderoz, 2017). We also know that negotiators are more
876	likely to reach mutually beneficial outcomes when both parties share information and make
877	tradeoffs (Smolinski & Xiong, 2020). Most negotiators are more effective when they prepare
878	concession plans and think in advance about the timing and magnitude of the concessions they
879	make—as well as the concessions they hope to elicit from other parties.
880	Choosing The Setting
881	Choosing the negotiation setting may be consequential. However, reflecting the dominant
882	experimental paradigms with which scholars have investigated negotiations, we know surprisingly
883	little about the influence of the negotiation setting, how negotiators choose their negotiation
884	settings, or how negotiators respond to invitations to negotiate in different settings. The limited
885	literature on this topic suggests that negotiators should choose their setting thoughtfully because
886	the negotiation setting is likely to influence how negotiators feel, what they learn about their
887	counterparts, and their negotiated outcomes (Brown & Baer, 2011; Fisher & Ury, 1981; Thompson et
888	al., 2010).
889	In practice, negotiations occur in a variety of places. Negotiators may choose to meet in an office
890	conference room, or they may complete a negotiation by phone or email; alternatively, negotiators
891	may convene in settings such as entertainment or sporting venues (e.g., on the golf green),
892	restaurants, bars, and even strip clubs (Schweitzer & Kerr, 2000). These settings can create
893	opportunities for rapport building, though they also present potential challenges. For example,
894	when meeting at a bar, negotiators are likely to consume alcohol. Depending on the amount of
895	alcohol that the parties consume—along with the food they have eaten and their relative
896	experience with alcohol—this could lead to certain advantages and disadvantages in a negotiation
897	(Morewedge et al., 2014; Schweitzer & Gomberg, 2001). Accordingly, rather than giving little
898	thought to the negotiation setting, deliberately choosing an ideal setting is a key step in the
899	preparation process.
900	Prior work on the negotiation setting has focused on whether negotiators should meet in their own
901	offices or in their counterpart’s office. Fisher and Ury (1981) suggest that negotiators meet in their
902	counterpart’s office, as this setting affords an opportunity to learn more about the other party.
903	Personality research supports this intuition because the way in which people organize their
904	personal spaces (e.g., number of photos, decoration style, level of tidiness) signals information about
905	their personality (Gosling et al., 2002). However, conducting a negotiation in a familiar environment
906	can confer advantages (Thompson et al., 2010). Specifically, negotiating in a familiar space makes
907	negotiators feel more comfortable, more confident, and better equipped to negotiate successfully
908	(Brown & Baer, 2011; Chu et al., 2005). For example, negotiators with “home field advantage”
909	outperformed their counterparts in a distributive negotiation, which may also reflect a visitor
910	disadvantage (Brown & Baer, 2011).
911	Pre-Negotiation Meetings
912	Though leading scholars have identified setting the stage as the most important negotiation phase
913	(see Fisher et al., 2011; Malhotra & Bazerman, 2007; Thompson, 2015), fundamental questions about
914	setting the stage for negotiations remain unexplored. For instance, we know surprisingly little
915	about how people actually prepare for negotiations—both in negotiation experiments and in the
916	field (Malhotra, 2015; Thompson et al., 2010). One exception involves work on topic selection during
917	pre-negotiation meetings. Research shows that conversations about shared superordinate goals (i.e.,
918	outcomes that both parties desire but cannot attain on their own) can build mutual trust and lead to
919	joint gains (Swaab et al., 2021).
920	Mindsets
921	People may go into their negotiations with different mindsets; how people select, encode, and
922	retrieve information can affect evaluations and behavior (Rucker & Galinsky, 2016). That is, the
923	mindsets negotiators adopt can predictably influence their behavior and their negotiated outcomes
924	(Trötschel et al., 2011). This stream of negotiation scholarship emerged alongside the judgment and
925	decision-making literature; as a result, much of this scholarship applies features of prospect theory
926	(Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) and related judgment biases. One key example involves framing
927	outcomes in terms of gains versus losses (Rabin, 1998; see Tversky & Kahneman, 1974).
928	Gain/loss
929	Robust scholarship has examined framing effects, which investigate the impact of highlighting a
930	situation as either a gain or a loss (Larrick & Blount, 1997; Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). This work
931	has found that when a potential agreement is framed as a relative loss (versus a relative gain),
932	negotiators become less cooperative, less likely to make concessions, and more likely to reach an
933	impasse (Bazerman et al., 1982; Bottom & Studt, 1993; De Dreu et al., 1994; 1995; Kahneman, 1992;
934	McCusker & Carnevale, 1995; Neale & Bazerman, 1985; Olekalns, 1994; 1997; Olekalns & Frey, 1994;
935	Schweitzer & DeChurch, 2001; Trotschel et al., 2013; Trotschel & Gollwitzer, 2007; Trotschel et al.,
936	2015). This is thought to occur because people experience loss aversion; in other words, they may
937	experience a loss as more painful than the corresponding gains are enjoyable, which prompts them
938	to avoid losses in general (De Dreu & McCursker, 1997; Meyerowitz & Chaiken, 1987; Schneider, 1992;
939	Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). Negotiator concessions (losses) “loom larger” than a counterpart’s
940	concessions (gains), making negotiation concessions very difficult.
941	Subsequent work also examined how framing specific moves within a negotiation (e.g., first offers),
942	rather than the negotiation itself, affects negotiator behavior. Specifically, framing a request as a loss
943	(or a request for resources) rather than a gain (or an offer of resources) induces greater concession
944	aversion, and thus, fewer counterpart concessions (Trotschel et al., 2015; Majer et al., 2020). In this
945	way, framing a move as a request (loss) rather than an offer (gain) can eliminate or reverse the
946	anchoring effect that occurs from first offers and ultimately lead to stronger counteroffers (Majer et
947	al., 2020). That is, by framing negotiation outcomes in terms of minimizing costs (losses) or
948	maximizing profits (gains), negotiators can influence both the negotiation process and the
949	negotiation outcomes (De Dreu et al., 1994; Levin et al., 1998; Pinkley & Northcraft, 1994; Bazerman
950	et al., 1985).
951	Asking frames and conflict frames
952	Negotiation scholarship has also considered other types of frames. For example, framing a
953	negotiation as an opportunity to ask (rather than negotiate) mitigated women’s relative aversion to
954	initiating a negotiation (Small et al., 2007).
955	Other scholarship identified conflict frames (Pinkley, 1990). For example, people may perceive
956	negotiations through a collaborative lens (a cooperative frame) or a competitive lens (win/lose
957	frame). Research shows that loss framing can cause negotiators to be more likely to adopt a
958	competitive frame (Schweitzer & DeChurch, 2001), which in turn can promote deception.
959	Construal level
960	One mindset that negotiation scholars have investigated quite extensively is construal level.
961	Construal level theory (Liberman & Trope, 2008; Trope & Liberman, 2003; 2010) proposes that
962	people’s mental representations may vary from abstract (i.e., high-level) to concrete (i.e., low-level)
963	representations. Abstract thinking (e.g., seeing the forest but not the trees) differs greatly from
964	concrete, detailed thinking (e.g., seeing individual trees but losing sight of the forest) (Burgoon et al.,
965	2013; Rosch, 1975; Rosch et al., 1976; Trope & Liberman, 2003; 2010; see Ledgerwood et al., 2010).
966	Construal level is impacted by the psychological distance that people perceive to have between a
967	focal object and objects or events at farther distances. Psychological distance has temporal (present
968	vs. future), spatial (near vs. far), and social (in-group vs. out-group) dimensions. For example,
969	negotiation scholars have induced psychological distance using a time-delayed outcome (Okhuysen
970	et al., 2003), or by having participants write about temporally close or distant events (De Dreu et al.,
971	2009).
972	Negotiation scholarship has found that higher-level or abstract (vs. low-level or concrete) construal
973	may prompt negotiators to act more cooperatively and achieve better joint outcomes (De Dreu et al.,
974	2009; Giacomantonio et al., 2010; Henderson et al., 2006; Henderson & Trope, 2009; Kortenkamp &
975	Moore, 2006; Okhuysen et al., 2003; Stillman et al., 2018; Wening et al., 2016; see Wiesenfeld et al.,
976	2017). This is thought to occur because higher levels of construal enable negotiators to take a “big-
977	picture” perspective and focus on multiple issues rather than single issues (Henderson et al., 2006;
978	Henderson & Trope, 2009). In addition, higher levels of construal allow negotiators to exchange
979	information more thoroughly (Wening et al., 2016) and focus more on their long-term relationship
980	with the other negotiating party (or parties) (Wiesenfeld et al., 2017).
981	Regulatory fit
982	Another mindset negotiation scholars have considered is “regulatory focus,” whether people are
983	primarily focused on gaining something valuable versus avoiding the loss of something valuable
984	(Higgins, 1998). For example, scholars have instructed negotiators to think about (a) “behaviors and
985	outcomes [they] hope to achieve” and how they could “promote these behaviors and outcomes”
986	(promotion mindset), and (b) “negotiation behaviors and outcomes [they] seek to avoid … and how
987	[they] could prevent these behaviors and outcomes” (prevention mindset) (Galinsky et al., 2005, p.
988	1092). Both Galinsky et al. (2005) and Peng et al. (2015) found that negotiators instructed to adopt a
989	promotion mindset attained better negotiated outcomes than those instructed to adopt a
990	prevention mindset. Apparently, negotiators who adopt a promotion-oriented mindset are better at
991	creating and claiming value than prevention-oriented negotiators. Quite possibly, people engaging
992	in Opportunity Negotiations, compared to Dispute Negotiations, may be more likely to adopt a
993	promotion-oriented mindset. Future work is needed to explore this possibility and to deepen our
994	understanding of the relationship between a promotion-prevention mindset, gain/loss framing, and
995	conflict frames (e.g., Schweitzer & DeChurch, 2001).
996	Phase 1: Setting The Stage: Conclusion
997	The lack of research on negotiation preparation is striking. Scholars should investigate not only how
998	negotiators prepare, but also how different aspects of setting the stage can influence the negotiation
999	process and negotiated outcomes. Specifically, additional research is needed to investigate the
1000	following questions: As negotiators prepare, what factors moderate how effective they are at
1001	identifying key information that they should seek or conceal? In turn, what factors moderate
1002	which questions negotiators should ask or anticipate? Future research should also investigate
1003	preparation for making first offers, concession plans, and identifying key current and potential
1004	issues to add to a negotiation, as well as the interplay between making first offers and concessions
1005	on the exchange of information.
1006	Phase 2: Communicating
1007	In the communicating phase, negotiators interact with each other as they strive to achieve their
1008	goals. These goals may include building a relationship, learning information, or seeking an outcome
1009	that improves the status quo. The classic experimental paradigm scholars have used to study
1010	negotiations is well-suited to the study of communicating, which is the most investigated phase of
1011	the negotiation process (see Jang et al., 2018). This review highlights nine distinct elements of the
1012	communication process: Non-task communication, exchange of information, distributive and
1013	integrative bargaining, first offers, concessions, persuasion, trust, deception, and emotion. Below,
1014	each of these elements is considered in turn, though it is important to note that many negotiations
1015	will include only some of them; it is also important to recognize that the communicating phase does
1016	not occur linearly. That is, negotiators may skip some parts of the communicating phase—for
1017	instance, non-task communication—or they may go back and forth between parts, such as between
1018	persuasion and making concessions.
1019	Non-Task Communication
1020	Many negotiations begin with non-task communication, or communication that is not directly
1021	related to the task at hand (e.g., “How is your family?”). Scholars have studied the role of non-task
1022	communication in building rapport—both in negotiation settings and in related, competitive
1023	domains such as sales and detective-led interrogations (Morris et al., 2002; Galinsky & Schweitzer,
1024	2015). Non-task communication may cover a range of topics, including the weather, sports, and
1025	favorite foods. These discussions may take hours as individuals seek to build rapport with one
1026	another (Galinsky & Schweitzer, 2015). In negotiations, non-task communication may vary from
1027	short opening statements such as “How was your trip?” to touring sites together, sharing meals, or
1028	making rounds of toasts (Smolinski & Xiong, 2020; Schweitzer & Kerr, 2000).
1029	A few studies have explored non-task communication in negotiation, and this research suggests
1030	that it offers substantial benefits. Specifically, scholars have found that negotiators can derive
1031	substantial benefits by beginning a negotiation with rapport building by “schmoozing”—engaging in
1032	relationship-focused, non-task communication (Morris et al., 1999; Shaughnessy et al., 2015)—or via
1033	“cheap talk”—engaging in communication unrelated to the task at hand (Bottom et al., 2006). Non-
1034	task communication can enable parties to discover similarities in attitudes, values, and interests
1035	(Ferrin et al., 2008); it may also promote greater information exchange and cooperation (Bottom et
1036	al., 2006; Katz, 2015; Mislin et al., 2011; Morris et al., 2002), encourage more positive emotions (Moore
1037	et al., 1999; Morris et al., 2002; Tiedens et al., 1999), and facilitate trust (see Lu et al., 2017).
1038	Though this literature is underdeveloped in relation to the likely importance of non-task
1039	communication, scholars have linked this communication with negotiation outcomes (Morris et al.,
1040	2000). Specifically, studies have found that negotiators who engaged in non-task communication set
1041	more realistic goals, identified a larger range of possible outcomes, and were less likely to experience
1042	impasses during a negotiation (Moore et al., 1999; Morris et al., 2002; Thompson & Nadler, 2002).
1043	Exchange Of Information
1044	The second part of the communicating phase is the exchange of information. During this process,
1045	negotiators reveal and seek information. Typically, this exchange happens as negotiators ask and
1046	answer questions.
1047	Asking questions
1048	A key part of the information exchange process involves asking and answering questions. Scholars
1049	have asserted that negotiators should become “investigators” by asking questions to learn about
1050	their counterpart’s BATNA, reservation value, and interests (Malhotra & Bazerman, 2007). Of
1051	course, important information can be gathered while setting the stage for a negotiation, but the
1052	extent to which negotiators can learn relevant information through preparation is limited, and the
1053	exchange of information during the communicating phase is integral to gaining insights that can
1054	inform the exchange of offers.
1055	Negotiators should ask direct questions, even if they believe that the other party may not fully
1056	answer them. By doing so, they can elicit useful information (Huang et al., 2018; Minson et al., 2018;
1057	Schweitzer & Croson, 1999; Thompson & Hastie, 1990). Conversational norms may compel
1058	negotiators to answer questions, as people often feel a sense of responsibility to answer questions
1059	that they are asked (Mazar et al., 2008; Rogers & Norton, 2011; Wiltermuth et al., 2015). Interestingly,
1060	even sensitive questions (e.g., “How much money do you make?”) tend to elicit truthful or very
1061	informative responses—without causing the relational harm that question-askers fear (Hart et al.,
1062	2021; Minson et al., 2018). Even when negotiation counterparts do not answer questions, negotiators
1063	can learn significant information (John et al., 2016). For example, when a negotiation counterpart
1064	declines to answer whether they have another offer, the other party can still make useful
1065	inferences.
1066	When asking questions, negotiators should focus on key information that they intend to learn.
1067	Negotiators should also be mindful of how they phrase their questions (Fisher et al., 2011; Malhotra
1068	& Bazerman, 2007; Thompson, 2015). For example, negative-assumption questions—or questions
1069	that presume a problem (e.g., “How many accidents has the car been in?”)—are more likely to elicit
1070	truthful responses (Minson et al., 2018).
1071	A key part of the exchange of information process involves listening to how people answer
1072	questions, rather than simply focusing on “selling” (as many novice negotiators do). Listening to the
1073	other party’s interests, needs, priorities, and constraints will be vital in maximizing the value each
1074	party can create. Finally, negotiators should be aware of any assumptions that they may have when
1075	entering a negotiation; they should also ask questions that challenge these assumptions rather than
1076	assume they are correct and seek confirming evidence.
1077	Communicating information
1078	As negotiators share information with their counterpart, they may cue reciprocity and inspire their
1079	counterpart to share information in turn (Gouldner, 1960; Thibaut & Kelley, 1959). Of course, when
1080	sharing information, negotiators should do so strategically. As with making concessions, negotiators
1081	should ensure they are receiving information as they share information, and recognize the value of
1082	any information that they disclose.
1083	In general, negotiators should not reveal their reservation point to the opposing party (Raiffa, 1982;
1084	Thompson, 2015), as negotiators who reveal this information are likely to reach an agreement near
1085	that point. When facing the prospect of an impasse, however, disclosing a reservation price may
1086	improve the likelihood of reaching a deal.
1087	In multi-issue negotiations, negotiators should try to convey information about their relative
1088	priorities—without minimizing the importance of any one issue (Fisher et al., 2011; Thompson,
1089	2015). This allows negotiators to communicate truthfully about the issues that they value most,
1090	without providing an opportunity for their counterpart to gain an advantage. One approach to
1091	communicating relative priorities is to make simultaneous offers across multiple issues (Leonardelli
1092	et al., 2019). By assessing a counterpart’s preference for different proposals, negotiators can learn
1093	about the party’s preferences and priorities across contexts.
1094	When communicating information, negotiators should think about their goals for the conversation
1095	and how they might achieve them. Goals can be classified along two dimensions: informational (i.e.,
1096	a focus on giving and/or receiving accurate information) and relational (i.e., a focus on building the
1097	relationship) (Yeomans et al., 2022). By reflecting on both their own and their counterpart’s
1098	conversational goals, negotiators can choose effective communication strategies and more
1099	accurately interpret information from the other party. For example, if an opposing party has a high
1100	informational goal, they will likely provide accurate information by asking questions and
1101	exchanging information; conversely, if they have a low informational goal, they may conceal key
1102	information by dodging questions or sharing irrelevant, distracting information. A negotiator’s goals
1103	may differ depending on the type of negotiation.
1104	Distributive And Integrative Bargaining
1105	Distributive bargaining involves splitting a pie, whereas integrative bargaining involves both
1106	expanding and splitting a pie (see Table 1). Though the dichotomy between distributive and
1107	integrative bargaining has been carefully distinguished in negotiation experiments, this dichotomy
1108	may be less clear in practical settings.
1109	Distributive negotiations are characterized by several key features. They require concessions from
1110	both parties (Neale & Fragale, 2006; Thompson, 2006). Compared to integrative negotiations, they
1111	tend to be more contentious and adversarial (Adair & Brett, 2005; Brett & Thompson, 2016; Kong et
1112	al., 2014; Liu & Wilson, 2011; Olekalns & Smith, 2000; Weingart et al., 1990). Similarly, negotiators in
1113	distributive negotiations are more likely to adopt a win/lose mentality and try to claim as much
1114	value as they can. For example, in distributive negotiations, people are more likely to conceal
1115	information, reveal information selectively, make extreme first offers, make few or minor
1116	concessions, and show little concern for the other party. When negotiators focus on distributive
1117	issues, they often adopt a zero-sum approach that does not seek to “expand the pie” or reach
1118	integrative outcomes because these issues, on their own, inherently involve a loss to one party
1119	when the other party gains (Bazerman & Neale, 1983; Brett & Thompson, 2016; Kong et al., 2014; Liu
1120	& Wilson, 2011; Olekalns & Smith, 2000; Weingart et al., 1990). This self-interested approach may
1121	indicate greed to some extent; it has also been found to reflect a concern about a risk of exploitation
1122	(Kong et al., 2014). Typically, these negotiations are competitive and occur between parties with
1123	short-term relationships. Quite possibly, negotiators could reach more efficient agreements by
1124	identifying opportunities to transform a distributive negotiation into an integrative one. The path to
1125	do this is likely to involve building rapport, cultivating trust, and diminishing a counterpart’s
1126	concerns about exploitation, so that people are more likely to reveal information that leads them to
1127	discover integrative solutions.
1128	In contrast to distributive negotiations, people in integrative negotiations can create value by
1129	identifying mutually-beneficial trades. In these negotiations, parties can make concessions on issues
1130	that are less important to them in exchange for concessions on issues that they value more; this is a
1131	social exchange known as logrolling (Froman & Cohen, 1970). Compared to distributive negotiations,
1132	people involved in integrative negotiations are more likely to adopt a win/win mentality, cooperate,
1133	and embrace a problem-solving mindset (Adair & Brett, 2005; Brett & Thompson, 2016; Fisher et al.,
1134	1981; Kong et al., 2014; Liu & Wilson, 2011; Olekalns & Smith, 2000; Weingart et al., 1990). For
1135	example, compared to people engaged in distributive negotiations, those engaged in integrative
1136	negotiations are more likely to openly share information about their interests and priorities with
1137	the other party, make reasonable first offers, engage in knowledge sharing, and show concern for
1138	the other party’s interests. In integrative negotiations, people are more likely to focus on their
1139	underlying interests (rather than positions) and consider multiple issues. Compared to distributive
1140	negotiations, integrative negotiations tend to be more cooperative (and more likely to occur
1141	between parties with longer-term relationships).
1142	Creative negotiators can make almost every distributive negotiation an integrative negotiation by
1143	adding an issue. For example, salary negotiations may include different start dates, purchasing
1144	negotiations may include bulk discounts, and home purchases may include keeping some of the
1145	client’s existing furniture. Adding issues can transform a distributive negotiation an integrative one
1146	—that is, one in which both parties can achieve gains from the negotiation. This process may also
1147	help to transform perceptions of the negotiation process, shifting the negotiation from a purely
1148	competitive (fixed-pied) process to a more collaborative one.
1149	Rather than reflecting a dichotomy, distributive versus integrative negotiations may involve a
1150	continuum. First, even purely distributive negotiations feature an integrative opportunity—that is,
1151	if parties reach an agreement that benefits both sides. Second, many distributive negotiations can
1152	become integrative negotiations (by adding additional issues, for example). And third, many
1153	integrative negotiations have a dominant distributive issue, such as salary or price. The extent to
1154	which integrative negotiations are characterized by a dominant distributive issue reflects a
1155	continuum.
1156	Which issues to negotiate first
1157	The complexity of the negotiation, and of the relationship between counterparts, can determine
1158	which issues to negotiate first. Ideally, negotiators will exchange offers that include values for every
1159	issue. In many cases, however, this is difficult, and negotiators may choose instead to negotiate
1160	issues sequentially (one at a time).
1161	In contentious negotiations, negotiators may seek to reach agreement on an easy issue in order to
1162	build trust and momentum. In other cases, however, they may tackle the hardest issue first—
1163	because if a deal cannot be reached on the most contentious issue, the rest of the negotiation could
1164	falter. We know very little about the moderators that are likely to make one of these approaches
1165	more successful than the other. In addition, discussing multiple issues simultaneously—especially
1166	for complex negotiations—may be beneficial because it can help negotiators identify tradeoffs and
1167	ensure a non-zero-sum negotiation (Malhotra & Bazerman, 2007).
1168	The best approach may depend on context. For example, when relationship conflict is high, starting
1169	with an easy issue could be an effective way to build momentum and lay the foundation for a
1170	future agreement. Additionally, negotiating groups with lower power may prefer negotiating more
1171	consequential issues first, whereas groups with higher power generally prefer negotiating less
1172	consequential issues first to maintain their position (Kteily et al., 2013). In general, however, to reach
1173	efficient agreements, negotiators should consider the full set of issues together.
1174	Common interest issues
1175	Negotiations may involve compatible issues known as common interest or common value issues
1176	(Lax & Sebenius, 1986; Pruitt & Carnevale, 1993; Raiffa, 1982). In negotiations, individuals may feign
1177	interest in an issue that they know the other party values in order to gain concessions on other
1178	issues (O’Connor & Carnevale, 1997). For example, in a divorce negotiation, a father may feign
1179	interest in retaining custody of the children—not because he actually wants custody, but because
1180	he knows that he could concede this issue to gain concessions on other issues later on in the
1181	negotiation (e.g., who gets to keep the house, cars, and yacht). Thus, in some cases, negotiators
1182	should be cautious when thinking about expressing their preferences; they should also invest
1183	resources in gauging their counterpart’s preferences. The possibility of being exploited makes
1184	asking questions early (e.g., the buyer might ask the seller “What closing date do you prefer?”)
1185	especially important. Concerns about exploitation and feigned interest are lessened in collaborative
1186	contexts where people hold cooperative versus individualistic motives (O’Connor & Carnevale,
1187	1997).
1188	First Offers
1189	A key part of the communicating phase is the exchange of offers. A substantial literature has
1190	explored offers in negotiation. Almost all of this work, however, has focused on first offers. This
1191	research has found that first offers can exert a substantial influence on negotiation outcomes.
1192	Specifically, negotiators often achieve better outcomes when they make assertive first offers
1193	(Benton et al., 1972; Chertkoff & Conley, 1967; Galinsky & Mussweiler, 2011; Liebert et al., 1968); this
1194	is because first offers can anchor the negotiation and influence a counterpart’s expectations and
1195	concessions (Adair et al., 2007; Ames & Mason, 2015; Galinsky et al., 2005; Galinsky & Mussweiler,
1196	2001; Galinsky et al., 2002; Gunia et al., 2013; Neal & Bazerman, 1991; Sinaceur et al., 2013). Once
1197	anchored by a first offer, negotiators often fail to sufficiently adjust away from the anchor (Epley &
1198	Gilovich, 2001; Galinsky & Mussweiler, 2011; Jeong et al., 2020). Reflecting the robustness of these
1199	effects, scholars have documented such patterns across settings and cultures (Barry et al., 2015;
1200	Gunia et al., 2013).
1201	Making and responding to a first offer
1202	When making a first offer, negotiators should have sufficient knowledge of their bargaining zone.
1203	This can help them avoid making an offer that leaves value on the table, or that is so excessive that
1204	it prompts the other party to exit the negotiation (Lee et al., 2018; see Galinsky et al., 2009).
1205	Gathering information plays a critical role in finding the right balance. Scholars have suggested that
1206	negotiators use their aspiration price to inform their first offer and make aggressive first offers, but
1207	how this works in practice remains an open question (Benton et al., 1972; Chertkoff & Conley, 1967;
1208	Fisher et al., 2011; Malhotra & Bazerman, 2008; Thompson, 2015). Prior work has found that
1209	aggressive first offers are beneficial for several reasons (see Gunia, 2013). First, they anchor the
1210	negotiation and provide room for a negotiator to make concessions (increasing the other party’s
1211	perceptions that the negotiator is cooperative and boosting the likelihood of a better outcome).
1212	Second, an aggressive first offer allows negotiators to focus on their own aspiration price, while
1213	encouraging their counterpart to focus on their reservation price (Galinsky et al., 2002; Mussweiler
1214	et al., 2000). Conversely, by making less aggressive first offers, negotiators may attain poor
1215	outcomes, elicit obstinate behavior from their counterpart, and obtain small concessions (Chertkoff
1216	& Conley, 1967). This finding is consistent with work that has found that negotiators who express
1217	gratitude are more likely to be exploited by their counterparts than those who do not (Yip et al.,
1218	working paper).
1219	However, most findings that support an assertive first offer derive from negotiation experiments in
1220	which the parties have few options to leave the negotiation and seek other counterparts. That is, we
1221	know surprisingly little about when negotiators are most likely to walk away from a negotiation.
1222	For example, if a tourist ventures into an art gallery and asks about a painting, when will an
1223	aggressive first offer prompt them to visit the art gallery across the street? Reflecting this possibility,
1224	generous first offers can increase trust and elicit more generous responses from a counterpart
1225	(Jeong et al., 2020).
1226	In contrast to some popular press advice—“never make the first offer”— negotiators can make the
1227	first offer when they have a good sense of the bargaining zone. That is, they should only make the
1228	first offer when they know their own reservation price and also have a sense of their counterpart’s
1229	reservation price (see Gunia, 2013). This advice is consistent with related work that underscores the
1230	importance of asking questions and exchanging information, rather than jumping immediately to
1231	the exchange of offers. By delaying the exchange of offers, negotiators may exchange more
1232	information and ultimately reach more creative agreements (Sinaceur et al., 2013).
1233	We know little about how negotiators should react to first offers. One scholarly concern is that
1234	negotiators may become anchored on a counterpart’s first offer (Fisher et al., 2011; Malhotra &
1235	Bazerman, 2008; Thompson, 2015). Scholars have encouraged negotiators to avoid falling prey to
1236	anchoring, but there is minimal literature on how to do this. Some have suggested that negotiators
1237	respond to an assertive first offer with their own aggressive counteroffer (Lipp et al., 2023), and then
1238	bring up the possibility of working together to bridge the gap (see Figure 3 for a depiction of the
1239	exchange of offers). Additionally, perspective-taking may be an effective way to counter the
1240	anchoring effects of an opposing party’s first offer (Galinsky & Mussweiler, 2001). Yet throughout,
1241	preparation is an important stage of the negotiation process, helping negotiators avoid falling prey
1242	to anchoring.
1243	Figure 3 : The Negotiation Dance
1244	Note: In a distributive negotiation, Sellers and Buyers exchange offers. In this example, the Seller
1245	starts by offering to sell at P5, and the Buyer counters by offering to buy at P1. The seller then
1246	offers to sell at P4, the buyer offers to pay P2, and the parties ultimately agree on a final price of
1247	P3. Negotiation dances are often (but not always) characterized by monotonic concessions (e.g.,
1248	P3 < P4 < P5): larger concessions at the beginning of a dance (e.g., (P5-P4) > (P4 – P3)), followed by
1249	reciprocal concessions (e.g., (P5-P4) similar to (P2-P1)), with negotiators often splitting the
1250	difference at the end (e.g., P3 similar to (P4-P2)/2).
1251	Anchoring
1252	First offers influence final outcomes by shifting expectations and by anchoring a counterpart.
1253	Anchoring occurs when people overweigh the influence of an initial value (Klein et al., 2014;
1254	Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). In negotiations, first offers heavily influence perceptions of value and
1255	final prices (Whyte & Sebenius, 1997). Even phantom anchors—or aggressive offers that are
1256	immediately retracted—can influence negotiators (Bhatia & Gunia, 2018). For example, when a seller
1257	states, “I was going to ask for $10,000, but I can offer $9,000,” their counterpart may still be
1258	influenced by the $10,000 anchor and perceive the $9,000 offer as a discount. Phantom anchors can
1259	cause negotiation counterparts to make less aggressive counteroffers and enable negotiators to
1260	reach more favorable outcomes; however, negotiators who use phantom anchors may be perceived
1261	as manipulative (Bhatia & Gunia, 2018).
1262	Ranges
1263	Rather than offering a specific value (e.g., “I can sell the car for $37,000”), negotiators can use ranges
1264	(e.g., “I can sell the car for $35,000 to $40,000”). Several scholars have asserted that it is better to
1265	make a first offer with a specific value rather than a range, because specific values are more likely to
1266	be used as anchors—and because specific values signal that the negotiator is well-informed,
1267	deliberate, and competent (Mason et al., 2013; Loschelder et al., 2017; Janiszewski & Uy, 2008).
1268	However, other work suggests that precise offers may signal inflexibility (Lee et al., 2018). In
1269	addition, when negotiating with an expert who has a sense of the bargaining zone, an assertive
1270	specific value outside this zone may signal incompetence (Loschelder, 2016). Thus, ranges may be
1271	advantageous when negotiators lack a good sense of the bargaining zone and still want to signal
1272	flexibility.
1273	Using ranges in a first offer can convey both (1) an informational effect: the endpoints of the range
1274	signal a negotiator’s reservation price and can anchor the negotiation, and (2) a politeness effect: the
1275	range can dampen extreme offers and make extreme counteroffers seem less polite (Ames & Mason,
1276	2015). A “bolstering range,” or a range that starts with an aggressive first offer as the low point of the
1277	range and then goes higher, can yield both positive economic and positive relational outcomes. A
1278	“bracketing range,” meanwhile, or a range in which the aggressive first offer is in the middle, confers
1279	relationship benefits—but it does not yield economic benefits. In general, wide ranges do not lead to
1280	more favorable deals than narrow ones (Ames & Mason, 2015).
1281	Concessions
1282	When exchanging offers, negotiators make concessions to their counterpart (Pruitt, 1981).
1283	Concessions strongly influence the trajectory of negotiations, affecting both negotiator satisfaction
1284	and outcomes (Benton et al., 1972; Chertkoff & Conley, 1967; Yukl, 1974). We know surprisingly
1285	little, however, about concession patterns and how they influence economic and relational
1286	outcomes in negotiations.
1287	Though little empirical work supports this assertion, negotiators should anticipate both first offers
1288	and any concessions that they plan to make before they start a negotiation. That is, negotiators
1289	should identify key issues, issues that may be added to the negotiation, and potential concession
1290	plans as they prepare to negotiate. Ideally, negotiators should concede on the issues that are of least
1291	importance to them, make smaller concessions over the course of the negotiation, and ensure that
1292	every party is conceding, rather than making unilateral concessions. Though little empirical work
1293	supports these assertions, experimental work has shown that by making smaller concessions over
1294	time, negotiators signal to their counterparts that they are approaching their reservation price (Tey
1295	et al., 2021).
1296	Preparing to make concessions is generally difficult. Through the information exchange process,
1297	negotiators may learn about the issues that matter most to their counterpart, and subsequently
1298	identify opportunities to make concessions that their counterpart will value for the lowest
1299	reasonable cost.
1300	A few studies inform the art and science of making concessions, though further research is needed
1301	given the centrality of this topic to the negotiation process. Thompson (2015) suggests that when
1302	making concessions, negotiators should provide explanations. Very little empirical work supports
1303	or informs the concession-making process, but by justifying each concession, negotiators can
1304	highlight—and perhaps gain recognition for—the concessions that they make. Ultimately, such
1305	explanations may trigger reciprocity, resulting in better economic and relational outcomes. We
1306	know very little, however, about factors such as how negotiators should frame their concessions, or
1307	how often negotiators should revisit past concessions that they have made. One concern is reactive
1308	devaluation (Ross, 1995; Ross & Ward, 1995), which indicates that after making a concession, a
1309	counterpart may assume that the concession was easy to make.
1310	Negotiators should also consider the timing of their concessionary behavior. Importantly, they
1311	should avoid making quick concessions, because this may cause their counterpart to expect
1312	additional concessions (and reduce the likelihood of reciprocity) (Chertkoff & Conley, 1967;
1313	Komorita & Barnes, 1969; Pruitt, 1981; Siegel & Fouraker, 1960; Smith et al., 1982). Instead, negotiators
1314	should make gradual concessions throughout the negotiation in order to increase both parties’
1315	satisfaction (Kwon & Weingart, 2004).
1316	In general, concessions by one party prompt reciprocity (Benton et al., 1972; Chertkoff & Conley,
1317	1967). However, aspects of the negotiation itself are likely to affect concessionary behavior, and
1318	importantly, some features of the negotiation process may cause one party to make greater
1319	concessions than another. For example, negotiations with high time pressure typically increase
1320	concession making (Carnevale et al., 1993; Hamner, 1974; Lim & Murnighan, 1994; Pruitt & Drews,
1321	1969). In some cases, negotiators may even stall the negotiation process to gain a relative advantage
1322	(Kang et al., 2020).
1323	High time pressure can also create a mismatch in concessionary behavior between parties. There
1324	are many cases in which negotiators may be relatively advantaged by the passage of time because it
1325	benefits their but in some cases. In some cases, negotiators may stall the negotiation to create time
1326	pressure or gain a relative advantage.
1327	Persuasion
1328	Part of the communication process involves convincing a counterpart that they should accept less
1329	favorable terms. However, little negotiation scholarship has focused on influence and persuasion
1330	tactics. The influence and persuasion literatures in the context of social psychology and
1331	management feature extensive recommendations and applications. Specifically, there are many
1332	opportunities for scholars to advance public understanding of how negotiators can persuade their
1333	counterpart to reveal information or agree to a deal. For example, our knowledge of escalation of
1334	commitment, reciprocity, and the use of social comparisons in negotiation is limited (see Novemsky
1335	& Schweitzer, 2001; Malhotra & Bazerman, 2008; Thompson, 2015, for exceptions). In one
1336	investigation, negotiators were less persuasive when they added arguments while making their
1337	first offer (Maaravi et al., 2011).
1338	Additionally, negotiation scholarship has underexplored the influence of cues as a form of
1339	persuasion. In one important exception, artifacts, such as expensive clothing or a fancy car, were
1340	shown to signal wealth (and a higher willingness to pay) to a negotiation counterpart and
1341	influenced the types of offers negotiators received (Maaravi & Hameiri, 2019).
1342	Trust
1343	A major influence during the communicating phase is trust between negotiators. Both within and
1344	separate from the negotiation literature, scholars have extensively researched the notion of trust
1345	(Campagna et al., 2016; Gunia et al., 2011; Kong, 2015; Kong et al., 2014; Naquin & Paulson, 2003;
1346	Olekalns & Smith, 2005, 2007, 2009; Sinaceur, 2010). Building closely on prior work, trust is defined
1347	as one party’s willingness to be vulnerable to another based on positive expectations (Rousseau et
1348	al., 1999, p. 395). The core bases for trust are competence, benevolence, and integrity (Mayer et al.,
1349	1995); competence reflects perceptions of ability, benevolence reflects care and concern for others,
1350	and integrity reflects a commitment to values such as honesty and credibility (Colquitt et al., 2007;
1351	Mayer & Davis, 1999).
1352	Benefits of trust
1353	Trust leads to substantial benefits in negotiation. It promotes cooperative behavior and
1354	collaboration, all while decreasing competitive behaviors (Bottom et al., 2006; Butler Jr, 1999; De
1355	Dreu et al., 2003; Dirks & Ferrin, 2001; Ferrin et al., 2008; Gunia et al., 2011; Kimmel et al., 1980;
1356	Mislin et al., 2011; Pillutla et al., 2003; Lewicki & Bunker, 1996; see Kong et al., 2014). With high levels
1357	of trust, people attain better negotiation outcomes (Schurr & Ozanne, 1985; Mislin et al., 2011; Kong
1358	et al., 2014; Olekalns & Smith, 2007), higher post-negotiation satisfaction (Kong et al., 2014), and
1359	greater commitment to deal implementation (Bottom et al., 2006; Mislin et al., 2011).
1360	When facing a reticent negotiation counterpart, negotiators should seek to build trust. Some may
1361	feel anxious about the prospect of negotiation (Brooks & Schweitzer, 2011), and trust can help one
1362	party mitigate their counterpart’s fear of exploitation. This process may involve building rapport,
1363	engaging in non-task communication, sharing some information, and taking non-verbal
1364	communication steps such as shaking hands (Schroeder et al., 2019) or leveraging mimicry (Huffaker
1365	et al., 2011; Swaab et al., 2011; Ireland & Henderson, 2014; Maddux et al., 2008). Ultimately, these
1366	efforts can increase trust, feelings of like, and cooperation.
1367	Trust is an important ingredient in effective negotiations (Thompson et al., 2010; Bazerman & Neale,
1368	1992). When negotiating parties experience high levels of trust, they may feel more comfortable
1369	taking risks, including by sharing information and structuring creative solutions (e.g., paying
1370	someone in advance). However, people who misplace their trust are more vulnerable to exploitation
1371	(Kong et al., 2014; Yip & Schweitzer, 2015).
1372	Antecedents of trust
1373	Several studies have identified antecedents of trust. One factor is a history of positive interactions
1374	(Schilke et al., 2023). Though a history of positive interactions is important, many experiences
1375	reflect censored environments. For example, managers may only observe how hard their team
1376	works when they are in the same room as their employees. When managers are unable to directly
1377	observe their subordinates, they may presume that their employees are working just as hard as
1378	they were when they were directly observing them. If, however, employees work harder when
1379	they know that they are being observed (and less hard when they know that they are not being
1380	observed), manager observations may reflect a censored environment. In practice, many settings
1381	reflect such environments. The core problem is that people systematically misplace their trust by
1382	over-relying on the biased sample of what they observe, and by failing to imagine how differently
1383	people behave when they are not observed (Schweitzer & Ho, 2005; Schweitzer et al., 2018).
1384	In accordance with the importance of benevolence, people are far more trusting of others when
1385	they observe a commitment to the relationship. For example, when people engage in non-task
1386	communication in a negotiation (e.g., small talk), they engender greater levels of trust (Mislin et al.,
1387	2011; Morris et al., 2002). Similarly, expressing positive emotion (Dunn & Schweitzer, 2005; Mislin et
1388	al., 2015), and then taking actions that foster rapport, such as asking questions, sharing information,
1389	and demonstrating empathic concern, can further promote trust (Butler, 1999; Brooks et al., 2014; Lu
1390	et al., 2017).
1391	Assessing trustworthiness is difficult, and building trust takes time (see Schilke et al., 2023 for a
1392	review). Though people are sensitive to many trust cues, the extent to which a person is guilt-prone
1393	is particularly important; guilt-prone people (e.g., those who would feel very guilty if they spilled
1394	red wine on someone’s white carpet) are far more trustworthy than those who are less guilt-prone
1395	(Levine et al., 2018).
1396	Breaking and restoring trust
1397	Trust is frequently violated, both inadvertently and intentionally. In negotiations, trust is especially
1398	fraught, because nearly every negotiation involves elements of competition. In this context, many

negotiate directly and rationally. In face cultures (e.g., many East and Southeast Asian cultures), a
person’s self-worth is derived from their social interactions, and power is derived from a stable
hierarchy; in these cultures, people negotiate less directly, value humility, and seek to fulfill their
collective duty. In honor cultures (e.g., many Middle Eastern and Latin American cultures), a
