1400	threats (Mislin et al., 2011; Morris et al., 2002), and expressing negative emotion can all hinder trust
1401	(van Kleef et al., 2010). In negotiations, trust is often violated when people are caught lying
1402	(Schweitzer et al., 2005).
1403	Though the process is difficult, negotiators can take measures to repair trust (Lewicki & Brinsfield,
1404	2017; Gillespie & Dietz, 2009; Lewicki & Wiethoff, 2000). Two key steps negotiators can take to
1405	restore trust include (a) delivering an effective apology (Schweitzer et al., 2015), and (b) exhibiting a
1406	consistent set of trustworthy actions (Schweitzer et al., 2006). A key component of an effective
1407	apology is a promise to change (Schweitzer et al., 2006). Tailoring the apology to the context and
1408	making credible attributions are equally critical (Kim et al., 2006).
1409	Deception
1410	Deception represents a particularly important challenge in negotiations. Since negotiations are
1411	characterized by information asymmetries and information dependence (Murnighan et al., 1999;
1412	Schweitzer & Croson, 1999; Schweitzer & Hsee, 2002), negotiators can gather a great deal of
1413	information as they prepare to negotiate—yet almost every negotiation includes unique information
1414	that individuals can only glean from the negotiation process itself. In many cases, negotiators can
1415	gain an advantage—at least in the short-term—by misleading a counterpart. As a result, deception is
1416	common in negotiations (Gaspar & Schweitzer, 2013; Gaspar & Schweitzer, 2021; Glac et al., 2014;
1417	Gunia & Levine, 2019; Koning et al., 2011; Kray et al., 2014; Minson et al., 2018; Rees et al., 2019;
1418	Tenbrunsel, 1998).
1419	Deception is defined as any communication intended to mislead another party (Gaspar et al., 2015;
1420	Gaspar et al., 2022). In negotiations, some types of deception are more serious than others.
1421	Misrepresenting a budget or bottom line, for example, is so common that it is almost expected in a
1422	negotiation context (e.g., “I can’t pay more than $200!” when the party can actually pay $250).
1423	Misrepresenting a material fact on which the counterpart relies, however, may constitute fraud
1424	(Shell, 1991). It is worth noting that there are many types of deception between these two extremes
1425	(see Lewicki & Robinson, 1998; Lewicki & Stark, 1996; Robinson et al., 2000; Schweitzer & Hsee,
1426	2002). In negotiations, deception typically involves misrepresenting information, but it may also
1427	involve emotional misrepresentation (Kang & Schweitzer, 2022; Gaspar & Schweitzer, 2013; Fulmer
1428	et al., 2009).
1429	Verbal deception
1430	Most prior work has studied verbal misrepresentation with text that misrepresents the true state of
1431	the world (e.g., “The car has never been in an accident”; O’Connor & Carnevale, 1997; Shell, 1991;
1432	Lewicki & Robinson, 1998; Robinson et al., 2000). In negotiations, people may misrepresent different
1433	types of information, from their budget limit or their intentions, to fundamental facts of the case.
1434	Scholars have also distinguished lies based on the types of statements that deceivers use. Lies of
1435	commission are active misstatements (e.g., “I have no plans to hire non-union workers for this
1436	project” when the opposite is true; see Lewicki & Robinson, 1998; Lewicki & Stark, 1996; Robinson et
1437	al., 2000). Lies of omission, meanwhile, involve a failure to disclose pertinent information. For
1438	example, a negotiating party may assume that their counterpart has no plans to hire non-union
1439	workers. The counterpart may know that the other party holds this mistaken impression and
1440	intentionally fail to correct it. In this case, the negotiator has lied by omission and is generally
1441	considered less culpable than if they had lied by commission; people targeted by lies of omission
1442	may share a greater portion of responsibility for the deception (Ren et al., 2022; Schweitzer &
1443	Croson, 1999).
1444	Other work has considered different forms of deception. Paltering, for example, involves the
1445	misleading use of truthful statements to create a false impression. For example, suppose that a
1446	union representative is concerned that the manager will hire non-union workers in the coming
1447	year. In this example, further suppose that the manager does intend to hire non-union workers, but
1448	that they have not hired non-union workers in the past. If the manager simply tells the union
1449	representative, “I have never hired non-union workers in the past” the manager is paltering. The
1450	manager is making a statement that is technically true, but misleading.
1451	Negotiators who engage in paltering perceive their own behavior as more ethical than if they had
1452	lied by commission (after all, they did not say anything untrue). However, targets of paltering hold
1453	deceivers just responsible as do targets of lies by commission (Rogers et al., 2017).
1454	Dodging involves a topic switch (e.g., when asked, “Do you plan to hire non-union workers?” the
1455	negotiator may reply, “Union labor helped to build some of the most important landmarks in this
1456	city”; Rogers & Norton, 2011). By dodging the actual question, respondents may shift the direction of
1457	the conversation. Related work has identified deflection, which is similar to dodging but involves
1458	the use of a question (e.g., when asked, “Do you plan to hire non-union workers?” the negotiator
1459	may reply, “Do you have family members who were part of local unions in this city?”; Bitterly &
1460	Schweitzer, 2020). People typically feel compelled to answer direct questions, so deflection is a
1461	particularly useful tactic in redirecting a conversation. Similar to lies of omission, people generally
1462	hold deceivers less responsible (and targets of deception more responsible) when they mislead
1463	people by dodging or paltering (Ren et al., 2022).
1464	Emotional deception
1465	Emotional deception is common in negotiations and occurs when people intentionally express an
1466	emotional state that is different from how they actually feel (Barry, 1999; Barry & Rehel, 2014;
1467	Fulmer et al., 2009; Gaspar et al., 2021; Campagna et al., 2016; Cote et al., 2013; Kang & Schweitzer,
1468	2022; Andrade & Ho, 2009). This is very different from how people misrepresent their emotions
1469	outside of a negotiation context. In general, people seek to up-display feelings of happiness and
1470	down-display feelings of anger; in negotiations, however, the opposite is true (Kang & Schweitzer,
1471	2022). For example, after receiving a generous offer, many negotiators may seek to display less
1472	happiness than they truly feel. Similarly, after receiving a mediocre offer, negotiators may display
1473	more anger than they actually feel. Interestingly, people consider emotional up-displays, or the
1474	exaggerated expression of a felt emotion, less ethical and less honest than emotional down-displays,
1475	or the diminished expression of a felt emotion (Kang & Schweitzer, 2022).
1476	Impact of deception
1477	In general, detecting deception is difficult (Bond & DePaulo, 2006). As a result, deception can
1478	profoundly influence the negotiation process and negotiated outcomes (Gaspar et al., 2019; Barry &
1479	Rehel, 2014; Gaspar & Schweitzer, 2013). Deception exerts a great deal of influence when it goes
1480	undetected, as people in such situations rely on inaccurate information. In addition, deception
1481	exerts a great deal of influence when the other party detects it, because it harms trust, elicits
1482	retaliatory behavior (Bowles et al., 2000; Brandts & Charness, 2003; Croson et al., 2003; Schweitzer &
1483	Croson, 1999; Wang et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2011), and is more likely to rupture relationships
1484	(Rogers et al., 2017; Campagna et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2020; Bowles et al., 2000; Schweitzer et al.,
1485	2006; Boles et al., 2000; Cote et al., 2013; Naquin & Paulson, 2003; Wang et al., 2009). The magnitude
1486	of the relational harm is typically linked to the severity of the deception, though even mild forms of
1487	deception can harm relationships (Bitterly & Schweitzer, 2020; Rogers et al., 2017).
1488	When targets detect deception, the perceived intent of the deception matters (Gaspar et al., 2019). In
1489	some cases, deception can strengthen relationships, such as when targets perceive the deception to
1490	be prosocial, or kind to the target (e.g., “Thank you for this perfect gift”; Levine & Schweitzer, 2015).
1491	However, self-serving deception—or deception that benefits the deceiver and exploits the
1492	counterpart (Erat & Gneezy, 2012; Gneezy, 2005)—is more common in negotiations, and it is this
1493	form of deception that consistently harms relational outcomes.
1494	When deception goes undetected, the deceiver may be able to extract concessions from their
1495	counterpart (Schweitzer et al., 2005; Rogers et al., 2017; Boles et al., 2000; Croson et al., 2004;
1496	Schweitzer et al., 2006; see Gaspar et al., 2022; Gaspar et al., 2019). This reinforces many negotiators’
1497	deceptive behaviors, making them more likely to leverage similar tactics in a future negotiation
1498	round (Ruedy et al., 2013; Vincent et al., 2013; Lewicki, 2012; see Gaspar et al., 2019).
1499	Antecedents of deception
1500	Reflecting the prevalence and importance of deception in negotiations, several studies have
1501	identified important antecedents of deception. One factor that makes negotiators more likely to
1502	engage in deception is feeling as though they were treated unfairly in the past (Schweitzer &
1503	Gibson, 2008). A second factor is the perception that a negotiation counterpart is a competitor
1504	rather than a collaborator (Schweitzer et al., 2005). Of course, negotiating parties both cooperate and
1505	compete with their counterparts (Galinsky & Schweitzer, 2015)—but some features of the
1506	negotiation process can make collaboration or competition more salient. For example, when a
1507	counterpart engages in trash talking, which can trigger feelings of rivalry, the other party is more
1508	likely to use deception (Yip et al., 2018). This finding is consistent with the notion that we are more
1509	likely to deceive a rival (Kilduff et al., 2016), and more likely to use deception when our motives are
1510	primarily selfish rather than prosocial (Steinel & De Dreu, 2004).
1511	Emotions, both felt and expressed, also influence the use of deception. Related to the perception of
1512	competition, researchers have found that people were more likely to lie to a negotiation counterpart
1513	when they felt envy (Moran & Schweitzer, 2008). In other work, people were more likely to use
1514	deception when they felt angry (Yip & Schweitzer, 2018) or anxious (Kouchaki & Desai, 2015).
1515	Additional literature has found that we are more likely to deceive people who express high levels of
1516	happiness (Barasch et al., 2016) or gratitude (Yip et al., 2018). Other work has also revealed that
1517	people are more likely to lie when they feel high levels of confidence (Gaspar & Schweitzer, 2021)
1518	and lower levels of guilt (Cohen et al., 2012; Morse & Cohen, 2019).
1519	Avoiding deception
1520	To curtail the risks of being deceived, scholars recommend asking direct questions that elicit honest
1521	answers (Schweitzer & Croson, 1999; Minson et al., 2018; VanEpps & Hart, 2022). In these situations,
1522	the types of questions matter. General questions (e.g., “What can you tell me about the car?”), and
1523	those that surmise the absence of a problem (e.g., “There aren’t any problems with the car, are
1524	there?”), are less effective in eliciting the truth than those that presume a problem (e.g., “What
1525	problems have you had with the car?”; Minson et al., 2018). Negotiators should also seek information
1526	from multiple sources and ask follow-up questions. For example, fraud investigators, in addition to
1527	meeting with a suspicious claimant, may talk with other people; this, along with gathering physical
1528	evidence, can inform the questions that they ask and their assessment of whether their counterpart
1529	is lying (Warren & Schweitzer, 2018). Negotiators in the field should similarly seek out information
1530	from sources, and engage in a conversation with their counterpart, to curtail their risk of being
1531	deceived.
1532	Emotion
1533	How people communicate in negotiations may be just as important as the language they use.
1534	Specifically, the way people experience and express emotion can greatly impact the negotiation
1535	process and negotiated outcomes.
1536	Experiencing emotions
1537	The experience of emotion can substantially influence a negotiation. The most common emotion
1538	people feel in anticipation of a negotiation is anxiety (Brooks & Schweitzer, 2011). Anxiety
1539	undermines confidence, and in negotiations, it may cause negotiators to lower their expectations,
1540	make less aggressive first offers, and attain worse outcomes (Brooks & Schweitzer, 2011).
1541	Other research has found that feeling positive affect can boost cooperation, trust, integrative
1542	behavior, and joint gains (Anderson & Thompson, 2004; Carnevale & Isen, 1986; Forgas, 1998). In
1543	contrast, feeling negative affect can lead to more aggressive first offers and greater competitiveness
1544	(Baron et al., 1990; Forgas, 1998; Knapp & Clark, 1991; Kassinove et al., 2002). Scholars have also
1545	investigated other emotions: Feeling compassion can lead to greater concern for others and promote
1546	joint gains (Allred et al., 1997), feeling guilty may encourage negotiators to be more cooperative
1547	(Ketelaar & Au, 2003), and feeling threatened can increase negotiator stress and lead to worse
1548	outcomes (Brooks, 2014; O’Connor et al., 2010).
1549	Expressing anger
1550	The most studied emotion in the negotiation literature is anger (Adler et al., 1998; Fisher et al., 1990;
1551	Gaspar & Schweitzer, 2013). Anger is closely associated with the negotiation process, and even if its
1552	expression is rare, it may be a particularly influential emotion in affecting negotiated outcomes
1553	(Campagna et al., 2019; Jang & Bottom, 2021; Sharma et al., 2020; Sinaceur & Tiedens, 2006; van
1554	Kleef et al., 2004; van Kleef et al., 2010).
1555	Anger may also offer benefits in a negotiation. By expressing frustration, negotiators can better
1556	extract concessions from their counterpart (Hershfield et al., 2012; Sinaceur & Tiedens, 2006;
1557	Sinaceur et al., 2011). Anger signals that a negotiator is dissatisfied with the negotiation process, and
1558	prior work has found that people may make greater concessions to an angry counterpart versus a
1559	neutral one (Sinaceur & Tiedens, 2006; van Kleef et al., 2004; 2010). However, this is less likely if the
1560	counterpart has a strong BATNA (Sinaceur & Tidens, 2006; van Kleef et al., 2004), or if the
1561	counterpart doubts the sincerity of the anger expression (Tng & Au, 2014).
1562	Expressing anger can also trigger negative counterpart behaviors. Specifically, after expressing
1563	anger, a counterpart may become more selfish, act more competitively, and engage in less
1564	integrative behavior (Allred et al., 1997; Butt et al., 2005). For example, when individuals are angry,
1565	they are more likely to reject unfair offers (Pillutala & Murnighan, 1996; Srivastava et al., 2009).
1566	Though many people seek to down-display their anger, the opposite may be true in a negotiation
1567	(Kang & Schweitzer, 2022), as negotiators seek to extract concessions (Adam & Brett, 2018) or mask
1568	feelings of anxiety (Brooks & Schweitzer, 2011).
1569	It is important to note that expressions of anger can cause relational harm (Campagna et al., 2016).
1570	By expressing anger, people are less likely to be trusted (Dunn & Schweitzer, 2005; Jang & Bottom,
1571	2022; van Kleef et al., 2015) and more likely to create a negative impression (van Kleef et al., 2004). In
1572	turn, negotiation counterparts are less willing to work with someone in the future if they express
1573	anger during a negotiation (Kopelman et al., 2006; van Kleef et al., 2004; van Beest et al., 2011).
1574	Expressions of anger may also trigger negative emotions in others (e.g., anxiety, fear, and anger:
1575	Lelieveld et al., 2012; Friedman et al., 2004; van Kleef et al., 2004). Targets of anger expressions may
1576	feel mistreated and seek to undermine the anger expressor (Wang et al., 2012). Further, expressions
1577	of anger can harm deal implementation (Jang & Bottom, 2022) making it not only more difficult to
1578	reach an agreement, but also more challenging to implement one (Friedman et al., 2004; Kopelman
1579	et al., 2006; Yip & Schweinsberg, 2017).
1580	In some cases, people who express anger later feel guilty about their behavior. As a result, they may
1581	make concessions that harm their goals (Campagna et al., 2019). However, this is more likely in
1582	negotiation experiments, and less likely among negotiators who intentionally up-display their
1583	expressions of anger.
1584	Expressing other emotions
1585	Scholars have also considered the influence of other emotions in negotiation. This work has found
1586	that expressing disappointment in a negotiation can induce guilt in the other party, leading them to
1587	behave more cooperatively (Lelieveld et al., 2012). Similarly, expressing sadness can elicit
1588	compassion and increase cooperation (Sinaceur et al., 2015).
1589	Expressing positive emotions may also lead to more positive impressions (Forgas & Bower, 1987) and
1590	engender trust (Mislin et al., 2011). Expressing positive emotions can trigger cooperation (van Kleef
1591	et al., 2004), making it more likely for the parties to reach a deal (Wilson et al., 2016). However,
1592	positive emotional expressions may reduce the magnitude of concessions others are willing to make
1593	(van Dijk et al., 2008; van Kleef et al., 2004). For example, expressing gratitude in a negotiation can
1594	cause a counterpart to engage in more aggressive and deceptive behavior (Yip et al., 2018).
1595	Changing emotional expressions
1596	Changing emotions during a negotiation may also influence negotiated outcomes (Filipowicz et al.,
1597	2011; Frijda, 1986; Kuppens et al., 2010; Scherer, 2009; Sinaceur et al., 2013). Emotional transitions
1598	can signal that the situation caused the emotional experience, rather than a person’s disposition. As
1599	a result, by changing emotional expressions during a negotiation, negotiators can signal to the other
1600	party that they caused the emotional expression. Reflecting this idea, one study found that
1601	participants made greater concessions to a counterpart who first experienced happiness and only
1602	later expressed anger versus a counterpart who consistently experienced anger (Filipowicz et al.,
1603	2011).
1604	Phase 2: Communicating: Conclusion
1605	Though most negotiation scholarship has focused on the communicating phase, several questions
1606	remain unanswered. Namely, research should investigate the limitations of the first-offer effect
1607	when people express a desire to exit the focal negotiation in search of new alternatives. Future
1608	research should also examine the limitations of a negotiator persuading (or being persuaded by)
1609	opposing parties during a negotiation, and of the complexity around when and how to make
1610	concessions as a negotiation unfolds.
1611	Phase 3: Closing
1612	In the closing phase, negotiators commit to an agreement. Though we may picture signing an
1613	agreement to close a negotiation, this stage often includes ritualistic behaviors such as a handshake,
1614	a bow, or a celebratory drink. In addition, the meaning and value of a signed contract is likely to
1615	vary a great deal across cultures and contexts. For example, the nature and importance of the
1616	closing stage of a negotiation may vary a great deal depending upon whether or not we are
1617	negotiating for a good or a service. If the negotiation involves the purchase of a good (e.g., a used
1618	car), the terms of a detailed contract are likely to reflect a complete understanding of the deal.
1619	However, when negotiating for a service (e.g., hiring a new employee), the closing stage of a
1620	negotiation represents just one part of a broader relationship. Yet in many cases, such as in
1621	negotiations for services, the process involves a long-term relationship; in places where contracts
1622	are not enforceable, the negotiation closing represents just one element of a broader relationship. In
1623	most negotiation studies, the completion of a deal sheet provided by the experimenter represents
1624	the closing phase of a negotiation. Correspondingly, we know relatively little about how to close a
1625	negotiation optimally.
1626	Terms Of The Deal
1627	When negotiators sign a binding contract to close a negotiation, there are several issues negotiators
1628	should consider. First, negotiators should ensure that the terms of the contract reflect the terms
1629	discussed during the negotiation. In some cases, during the closing phase of negotiations,
1630	negotiators intentionally change terms in the contract. When discovered, this can create significant
1631	conflict and rupture an agreement. Very little scholarship, however, has studied this.
1632	Second, during the closing phase of negotiations, some negotiators “nibble” at the agreement. That
1633	is, as negotiators finalize an agreement, some negotiators insist on additional concessions. Often,
1634	negotiators employ this tactic to extract additional concessions from a counterpart when they have
1635	additional leverage (e.g., a home seller might insist on additional concessions after the home buyer
1636	has put all of their belongings in a moving van).
1637	Third, contracts are likely to be incomplete. Even detailed contracts cannot cover every eventuality.
1638	As a result, negotiators with contracts should anticipate the possibility of renegotiating with their
1639	counterparts and value relational outcomes (e.g., maintaining trust with their counterpart in case
1640	they will need to negotiate again in the future).
1641	Subjective Value
1642	In addition to the deal terms, negotiators obtain a rich set of other outcomes from concluding a
1643	negotiation (Thompson, 1990). These include subjective-value outcomes, which include feelings
1644	about the instrumental outcome (e.g., outcome satisfaction, fairness), feelings about oneself (e.g.,
1645	saving face, meeting one’s standards), feelings about the negotiation process (e.g., fairness, voice),
1646	and feelings about the relationship between the negotiating parties (e.g., positive impressions, desire
1647	for a future relationship) (Curhan et al., 2006).
1648	Subjective value is important for several reasons. First, it can influence future outcomes (Curhan et
1649	al., 2006; Galinsky & Schweitzer, 2015). If negotiating parties establish a positive relationship, they
1650	can build relational capital, which makes both parties more willing to work together in the future.
1651	Additionally, negotiators who derive high subjective value from their negotiation experience
1652	typically enjoy more positive immediate outcomes from the negotiation (e.g., higher satisfaction
1653	with the negotiation process) and more positive long-term outcomes (e.g., lower turnover intention
1654	one year later; Curhan et al., 2009). Further, with positive subjective value, when negotiations
1655	involve services, negotiators are more likely to directly impact the economic value of an outcome
1656	(Hart & Schweitzer, 2022). For example, a hiring manager may benefit from hiring a new employee
1657	who is excited about their working relationship; this positive relationship may be even more
1658	important to long-term economic outcomes than the deal terms outlined in the signed contract.
1659	Failed Negotiations And Impasses
1660	Many negotiations end without an agreement. Reflecting the dominant paradigm that we have
1661	used to study negotiations—roleplay exercises with positive zones of agreement—many negotiation
1662	scholars have implicitly or explicitly characterized impasses as failures. In some cases, impasses
1663	really do reflect failures, including failures to learn information, identify opportunities for an
1664	agreement, and make compromises that could yield better joint gains. In these cases, learning from
1665	unsuccessful negotiations could be beneficial. For example, negotiators could learn important
1666	information about themselves and their negotiation style; alternatively, they could learn how to
1667	better discern cues from their counterpart.
1668	However, many negotiation impasses are not actually failed negotiations (see Kesner & Shapiro,
1669	1991; Schweinsberg et al., 2022). Negotiations may reach an impasse—wherein one or more parties
1670	ends the interaction because they could not come to an agreement (Schweinsberg et al., 2022)—for
1671	many reasons. There are three types of impasses: Wanted impasses are those in which both
1672	negotiators wanted the negotiation to end in an impasse, unwanted impasses are those in which
1673	neither party desired an impasse, and forced impasses are those in which only one party sought an
1674	impasse. In some cases, an impasse may be the best option for both parties. For example, both
1675	negotiating parties may be better off going with their BATNAs, or they may desire an impasse
1676	because they believe that revisiting the negotiation at a later date—when their party is better
1677	prepared for a deal—will yield better outcomes. The potential for instrumental negotiations, or
1678	those in which one party uses the negotiation process for an ulterior motive, such as to stall for time
1679	or extract information from a counterpart, is a key reason why one or more parties may end a
1680	negotiation (Kang et al., 2020).
1681	Closing: Conclusion
1682	This review highlights the limited attention that researchers have paid to the closing phase of
1683	negotiations and calls for scholars to investigate the intricacies surrounding the act of committing to
1684	a deal. Specifically, additional research is needed to explore the ways in which people commit to the
1685	terms of an agreement, the factors that influence the subjective value that negotiators experience
1686	during the closing phase, and the financial and interpersonal antecedents and consequences of
1687	impasses.
1688	Phase 4: Post-Negotiation
1689	Post-negotiation behavior is extremely important. In many domains—for example, when
1690	performing a service—the value of a negotiated agreement is created after the negotiation. In
1691	addition, behavior after a negotiation may include intentions to reengage with a counterpart in a
1692	future negotiation. As a result, the rapport negotiators develop through the negotiation process can
1693	have important downstream consequences.
1694	Post-Agreement Behavior
1695	In many negotiation contexts, post-negotiation behavior is a primary driver of economic value
1696	(Hart & Schweitzer, 2020; 2022). For example, after negotiating a new employee’s salary, the
1697	employee will perform work and exert effort that creates economic value for their manager.
1698	Notably, this is not how most experiments have studied negotiation. For example, in the popular
1699	negotiation exercise “New Recruit,” which involves hiring a new employee, the negotiation simply
1700	ends with a deal sheet asking participants about the terms of their deal—there is no post-negotiation
1701	stage.
1702	Hart and Schweitzer (2022) introduce the concept of ERRO (economic relevance of relational
1703	outcomes) to conceptualize the idea that relational outcomes impact economic outcomes. In “high
1704	ERRO” contexts, a counterpart’s post-negotiation behavior can greatly impact a negotiator’s
1705	economic value. For example, when a manager hires a new employee, the economic outcome of the
1706	negotiation is affected not only by the explicit terms of the deal (e.g., how much the manager pays
1707	the employee), but also by the employee’s post-negotiation behavior (e.g., how hard the employee
1708	works after the negotiation). In contrast, in “low ERRO” contexts, a counterpart’s post-negotiation
1709	behavior weakly affects the negotiator’s final economic outcome. For example, a buyer may
1710	purchase a vacuum or a new phone, and in these situations, the seller’s post-negotiation behavior
1711	has very little impact on the value that the buyer derives from the sale. In short, in high ERRO
1712	contexts, negotiators show greater relational concern, negotiate less competitively, establish
1713	stronger relationships with the other party, and positively motivate their counterpart’s post-
1714	negotiation behavior (ultimately resulting in economic benefits for the negotiator) (Hart &
1715	Schweitzer, 2022).
1716	Some work also suggests that simply engaging in a negotiation—rather than abstaining from a
1717	negotiation—can affect post-negotiation behavior (Hart & Schweitzer, 2020). Negotiations are
1718	mixed-motive interactions in that parties must navigate a blend of aligned and competing goals. In
1719	some cases, by engaging in a negotiation (particularly a distributive negotiation that focuses on the
1720	exchange of prices), negotiators highlight their conflicting interests in a manner that can harm post-
1721	negotiation motivation. This is a particular concern for services, where post-negotiation behavior
1722	creates extensive value. For example, potential negotiators may avoid negotiating the wage of a new
1723	babysitter. Instead of seeking better deal terms, the best course of action may be to avoid
1724	negotiating altogether.
1725	Negotiator Satisfaction
1726	Negotiator satisfaction is a meaningful predictor of a negotiator’s future behavior (Curhan et al.,
1727	2009; Novemsky & Schweitzer, 2004). There are several factors that influence negotiator
1728	satisfaction. One key factor is the subjective perception of a deal’s economic value. For example,
1729	negotiators are often dissatisfied if their first offer is accepted because they may believe that they
1730	could have attained a better outcome (Galinsky et al., 2002).
1731	Research has found that negotiator perceptions of a deal’s economic value are also influenced by
1732	the comparisons people make to evaluate their outcome (Novemsky & Schweitzer, 2004). That is,
1733	the satisfaction a negotiator may derive depends on several types of comparisons: (1) the
1734	comparison a negotiator makes between their own outcome and the outcome of their counterpart
1735	(e.g., a car buyer comparing their outcome to the seller’s profit; Gillespie et al., 2000; Loewenstein et
1736	al., 1999; Novemsky & Schweitzer, 2004), (2) the comparison a negotiator makes between their own
1737	outcome and the outcome they expected to attain (e.g., a car buyer comparing their actual outcome
1738	to their expected outcome; Oliver et al., 1994), and (3) the comparison a negotiator makes between
1739	their own outcome and the outcomes attained by those in a similar situation (e.g., a car buyer
1740	comparing their outcome to other car buyers’ outcomes; Novemsky & Schweitzer, 2004). For
1741	example, a negotiator’s aspiration and reservation prices may influence their satisfaction in that
1742	those with a low (vs. high) reservation and aspiration price, respectively, were more satisfied and
1743	felt more successful even with identical outcomes (Thompson, 1995). Additionally, negotiators who
1744	focus on their aspiration price typically attain better economic outcomes in negotiations, but they
1745	are less satisfied after the negotiation than those who focus on their BATNA (Galinsky et al., 2002).
1746	One implication is that negotiators could strategically shift their focus depending on the negotiation
1747	phase: Negotiators should focus on their aspiration price during the negotiation in order to reap the
1748	best outcome and focus on their BATNA after the negotiation in order to gain the most satisfaction
1749	(Galinsky et al., 2002). In practice, however, this may be difficult.
1750	Counterpart Satisfaction
1751	Managing the satisfaction of one’s counterpart is particularly important (Carnevale et al., 1982;
1752	Carnevale & Isen, 1986; Curhan et al., 2006; Curhan et al., 2009). A satisfied counterpart can increase
1753	commitment to an agreement and help negotiators build a favorable reputation. This can be done
1754	by managing the other party’s perceptions of the deal—by helping to convince the counterpart that
1755	they attained a favorable agreement, that they are respected, and that the outcome was equitable.
1756	Making sure that one’s counterpart is satisfied is also important because it will affect the party’s
1757	post-negotiation behavior, which can subsequently impact their future intentions and the
1758	negotiator’s own economic value (Hart & Schweitzer, 2020; 2022).
1759	Reputations
1760	Though most negotiation scholarship to date has focused on single-shot negotiations, a negotiator’s
1761	long-term reputation can influence the decision to enter a negotiation and ultimately drive the
1762	counterpart’s behavior. Many negotiations involve ongoing interactions (e.g., union-management
1763	negotiations or employee-boss negotiations) that enable potential negotiators to learn from others’
1764	experiences.
1765	A few studies have explored reputations in negotiation (see Tinsley et al., 2002). This work has
1766	studied the development of both negative (or difficult) and positive (or trustworthy) reputations. For
1767	example, after engaging in aggressive or competitive behavior, and after making an extreme offer,
1768	negotiators can gain a reputation that causes future negotiators to adopt a more confrontational
1769	approach, ultimately making future negotiations more difficult (Bhatia & Gunia, 2018; Campagna et
1770	al., 2016; Schweinsberg et al., 2012; see Huffmeier et al., 2014). Indeed, establishing a reputation as a
1771	competitive negotiator may cause negotiation counterparts to set higher aspirations and behave
1772	more contentiously (Galinsky et al., 2002; Tinsley et al., 2002).
1773	Conversely, a history of building relationships and trust can benefit a negotiator’s reputation and
1774	improve their long-term economic outcomes (Curhan et al., 2009; Glick & Croson, 2001; Kong et al.,
1775	2014). When interacting with a negotiator who has a positive reputation, the other party is more
1776	likely to share information (Tinsley et al., 2006).
1777	Repeated Negotiations
1778	Repeated negotiations are yet another under-investigated topic in negotiation scholarship. Often,
1779	rather than meeting for the first time, negotiation counterparts may convene to renegotiate an
1780	existing agreement. For example, airlines and pilots, as well as employees and managers, routinely
1781	renegotiate their contracts. Often, this occurs after a fixed period of time, or after discrete events
1782	(e.g., after an employee has received an outside offer).
1783	Relational concerns and trust are critical where repeated negotiations are concerned (Ferrin et al.,
1784	2008; Hart & Schweitzer, 2020; 2022; Lount et al., 2008). Negotiators can use the rapport and
1785	goodwill that they have accrued in a prior negotiation to help them in future negotiations.
1786	Additionally, if negotiators anticipate future negotiations with the same party, they might
1787	strategically make concessions to reap better outcomes later. Some work also suggests that the type
1788	of impasse that a prior negotiation ended on can affect behavior in a future negotiation
1789	(Schweinsberg et al., 2022).
1790	Stage 4: Post-Negotiation: Conclusion
1791	Post-negotiation feelings and behavior can play an important role in the subjective and economic
1792	outcomes people attain from a negotiation. Future research should investigate questions such as:
1793	What post-negotiation behaviors are most impactful, how can negotiators optimize post-
1794	negotiation behavior, how might negotiators maintain both their own and their counterparts’
1795	satisfaction during and after the negotiation, and what factors moderate subjective and economic
1796	outcomes of repeated negotiations?
1797	Phases Of Negotiation: Conclusion
1798	In this review, negotiations are conceptualized as having four distinct phases: setting the stage,
1799	communicating, closing, and post-negotiation. Most negotiation scholarship has focused on the
1800	communicating phase, and much of this work has examined the influence of first offers. This focus
1801	reflects, in part, the dominant paradigm we have used to study negotiations—namely, lab-based
1802	studies in which people are assigned roles, read background information, and asked to enact a
1803	negotiation. Future work should use additional methods to explore other stages of the negotiation
1804	process in greater depth.
1805	THE LIMITS OF WHAT WE KNOW
1806	Negotiation is important and complex in equal measure. This review concludes with a brief history
1807	of negotiation scholarship, additional thoughts on the limits of what we know, and a call for future
1808	negotiation research.
1809	Though humans have been negotiating for millennia, the academic study of negotiation is
1810	remarkably recent. Scholars have studied adjacent fields, such as conflict (a broader topic that
1811	encompasses goal conflict, emotional conflict, and war; Himes, 2008), but only (relatively) recently
1812	did Nash (1953) formalized the idea of mixed motive negotiations that involve both cooperation and
1813	competition. In 1982, Howard Raiffa published The Art and Science of Negotiation, a book that
1814	transformed the study of negotiation. As Keeney (2016, p. 215) explains, Raiffa “founded the
1815	discipline of negotiation analysis. Prior to that time, much of the knowledge about negotiations was
1816	basically art and folklore, with essentially no systematic structure or science.” In psychology, early
1817	negotiation research built on Raiffa’s (1982) framework and focused on cognitive biases (e.g.,
1818	anchoring, overconfidence; Galinsky & Mussweiler, 2001; Larrick & Wu, 2007). Subsequent work
1819	extended the study of negotiation to include a broader set of dynamics, including the influence of
1820	affect and emotion (e.g., anger, anxiety; van Kleef et al., 2004; Brooks & Schweitzer 2011) and key
1821	features of negotiation conversations (e.g., asking questions, speaking turns; Kwon & Weingart,
1822	2004; Minson et al., 2018).
1823	Negotiation scholarship, however, has developed across several disciplines, including
1824	communications (Putnam & Roloff, 1992), economics (Roth, 1985), legal scholarship (Wilkinson-Ryan
1825	& Small, 2008), and crisis negotiations (Vecchi et al., 2005). Each discipline has approached
1826	negotiations with a unique lens, but across these disciplines, scholars have wrestled with a common
1827	challenge: Negotiations are hard to study. It is difficult for scholars to insert themselves as observers
1828	in the midst of important business or political bargaining. It is similarly difficult to get complete
1829	transcripts and interviews of participants in these negotiations. As a result, negotiation scholars
1830	have worked to draw inferences from a single or small number of actual negotiations (Sebenius,
1831	1984), analyzed partial information gleaned from many negotiations (Schweinsberg et al., 2023), or
1832	relied on experimental simulations (Brown & Baer, 2011) to further our understanding of this topic.
1833	To this end, in social psychology, roleplay exercises represent the dominant paradigm scholars have
1834	used to study negotiations. Initially, social psychologists analyzed the roleplay exercises that they
1835	had conducted with their students; later, with increasing sophistication, they conducted negotiation
1836	simulations with lab-based and online participant samples. Results from these studies have helped
1837	to build knowledge and understanding of negotiations, but many questions involving this approach
1838	to studying remain unanswered. For example, by inviting participants to engage in a negotiation,
1839	we have learned very little about when or why people avoid or choose to negotiate. Table 2
1840	identifies several underexplored facets of negotiation, and future work should expand our
1841	understanding of several streams of negotiation scholarship.
1842	Table 2: Call for Negotiation Research
1843	Note. Though some scholarship has studied these topics, they are under-investigated.
1844	There are many important areas of negotiation research that merit additional attention. Several
1845	under-investigated topics are listed in Table 2. In addition to these topics, we call for future scholars
1846	to advance our understanding of cross-cultural negotiations (Gelfand et al., 2012). This work should
1847	study the intersection of individual characteristics in addition to culture (e.g., gender, ethnicity,
1848	culture, sexual orientation; Shan et al., 2019). Future work is also needed to expand our
1849	understanding of contextual factors, such as how the negotiation setting may influence the
1850	negotiation itself (Brown & Baer, 2011), or how alcohol may impact the negotiation process
1851	(Schweitzer & Kerr, 2000; Schweitzer & Gomberg, 2001).
1852	Further, future work should expand our understanding of emotion, trust, and deception in
1853	negotiations. It should also expand our understanding of the exchange-of-information process and
1854	how the exchange of offers affects relational outcomes. For example, whereas most emotion
1855	research in negotiations has focused on anger (Adler et al., 1998), there are substantial opportunities
1856	to build on a growing literature that has studied other emotions (see Lelieveld et al., 2012; Sinaceur
1857	et al., 2015; Yip et al., 2018). Many open questions remain, especially with respect to the most
1858	common negotiator emotions—excitement and anxiety (see Brooks & Schweitzer, 2011). Another
1859	fruitful avenue for research involves deepening our understanding of the most effective strategies
1860	for building trust (Mislin et al., 2011; Mislin et al., 2015), and the ways in which trust is broken
1861	(Schweitzer et al., 2005; van Kleef et al., 2010) and restored (Schweitzer et al., 2006) during a
1862	negotiation.
1863	Similarly, future work should expand our understanding of unethical behavior in negotiations.
1864	Prior work has studied unethical behavior almost exclusively with respect to deception, but many
1865	other types of unethical negotiator behavior exist as well—for example, engaging in insincere
1866	negotiations or negotiating in bad faith (Kang et al., 2020).
1867	Negotiations In The Wild
1868	Many of the gaps in our understanding reflect the paradigms we have used to study negotiation.
1869	Due to scholars’ dependence on laboratory-based experiments, we know surprisingly little about
1870	some of the most important features that influence negotiations. For example, though many of our
1871	most important negotiations involve people with substantial negotiation experience—and those
1872	with asymmetries in experience, such as negotiations to purchase a house (e.g., realtors vs. first-time
1873	home buyers), to purchase a car (e.g., car salespeople vs. buyers), to negotiate a salary (e.g., HR
1874	managers vs. new employees), or to negotiate a merger between companies (e.g., business executives
1875	vs. their lawyers)—we know surprisingly little about negotiator expertise. Similarly, we know very
1876	little about what happens after a negotiation concludes; our knowledge of how repeated
1877	negotiations unfold is equally limited, and we know little about team and multiparty negotiations.
1878	Future negotiation scholarship should address these critical gaps in our knowledge.
1879	We also know little about naturalistic features of negotiation. This leads to key questions involving
1880	topics such as how negotiations unfold over prolonged periods of time. In addition, how do prior
1881	negotiations and existing relationships influence the negotiation process? What happens when
1882	some members of a negotiation team have worked together, but others have not?
1883	Some of the most important forces that influence negotiation occur away from the negotiation
1884	itself. For example, we know little about how to prepare for a negotiation, how to improve a
1885	BATNA, what pre-meetings to schedule before a multiparty negotiation, or how negotiations
1886	influence post-negotiation behavior. Consequently, negotiation scholarship should extend
1887	investigations to field settings in order to fill such gaps in our understanding.
1888	Technological Advancement And Building Bridges In Negotiation Scholarship
1889	Technology has transformed the way negotiations are conducted, and this is reflected in research.
1890	Whereas most early work focused on face-to-face negotiations, more recent scholarship has
1891	examined email, text, and video negotiations. Several studies have investigated how negotiating
1892	face-to-face compares to negotiating via email, text, or video conference (Geiger, 2020; Schweitzer et
1893	al., 2002). In general, face-to-face negotiations yield more efficient outcomes (Geiger, 2020).
1894	Specifically, face-to-face negotiations may require less time to finalize an agreement than text-based
1895	mediums (Galin et al., 2007), and compared to email, face-to-face negotiations engender greater
1896	trust (Lu et al., 2017; Naquin & Paulson, 2003). Text-based negotiations, however, have important
1897	benefits in affording asynchronous and economical communication. In addition, text-based
1898	negotiations may enable negotiators to develop higher construals and ultimately attain more
1899	efficient outcomes (Friedman & Belkin, 2013).
1900	Overall, scholarship has identified relatively few differences in negotiation across mediums (see
1901	Geiger, 2020). The differences scholars have identified appear to relate to moderators, such as the
1902	negotiating party’s cooperative orientation (Swaab et al., 2012), culture (Rosette et al., 2012), and
1903	whether the negotiating parties have a personal relationship (Moore et al., 1999). Comfort with the
1904	medium (Geiger & Parlamis, 2014) and intent to use deception (Schweitzer et al., 2002) are additional
1905	differences to consider across mediums.
1906	One challenge—and opportunity—in studying the interplay between negotiation and technology is
1907	the continued evolution of technology-associated norms. For example, Schweitzer et al. (2002)
1908	studied video negotiations circa 2000. At the time, video negotiations were novel and required
1909	specialized equipment in a dedicated room. Norms regarding video negotiations shifted
1910	dramatically in the ensuing decades, but scholars have not sufficiently revisited the interplay
1911	between technology and negotiations.
1912	Another direction for future work is the investigation of the mixed use of communication media.
1913	For example, negotiators may meet in person at one point in time, and then continue to negotiate
1914	via video at a second point in time. Meeting in person may help negotiators build and maintain
1915	trust, and future work can explore the optimal mix for meeting in person and via video over time.
1916	Emerging technologies have created a growing number of opportunities for negotiators. For
1917	example, negotiators may use training software to prepare for a negotiation or get feedback on their
1918	negotiation skills (Johnson et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2019; see Dinnar et al., 2021). Other
1919	technology enables negotiators to change their appearance or speaking style (Baten & Hoque, 2021).
1920	Technological innovations have also vastly improved negotiators’ ability to communicate with
1921	people in different languages, in real time, across far distances. And of course, developments in
1922	artificial intelligence are creating new avenues for training in negotiation, such as using bots to
1923	prepare and debrief negotiations, providing personalized feedback, and even providing mediation
1924	services.
1925	In addition to helping negotiators prepare and make decisions within their negotiations, new
1926	technologies also create opportunities for negotiation scholars. For example, scholars can research
1927	negotiations with chatbots built with artificial intelligence and use natural language processing and
1928	machine learning to analyze conversational data at scale. In contrast to early work that analyzed
1929	negotiation texts with human coding (see Weingart et al., 2004; Schweitzer & Gomberg, 2001), more
1930	recent technological advancements enable us to analyze massive amounts of text quickly (Kosinski,
1931	2024). This line of inquiry connects with a growing literature (Brooks et al., 2019; Reece et al., 2023;
1932	Yeomans et al., 2022) that highlights our need to better understand how features of conversations
1933	influence the negotiation process and negotiated outcomes (Hart et al., 2021; Minson et al., 2018).
1934	Similarly, advancements in emotion coding and physiological measures offer new paths to deepen
1935	our understanding of emotion and deception in a negotiation context.
1936	CONCLUSION
1937	Over the past 50 years, the study of negotiations has evolved from examining simple, abstract
1938	choices to harnessing sophisticated experimental designs and large-scale data analysis (Boothby et
1939	al., 2023; Raiffa, 1982; Schweinsberg et al., 2023). This scholarly progression has established core
1940	negotiation principles, identified crucial contextual factors and moderators, and informed practical
1941	strategies that comprise the backbone of countless courses, resources, and popular publications.
1942	However, despite the significant body of negotiation scholarship, our understanding of this
1943	complex, consequential, and ubiquitous phenomenon is still developing. The intricacies of human
1944	interactions, combined with ever-evolving social norms and advancements in technology and
1945	research methods, ensure that negotiation scholars will continue to uncover insights that will
1946	shape our personal and professional lives for decades to come.

Though the process is difficult, negotiators can take measures to repair trust (Lewicki & Brinsfield,
